en: He whom the Lord of the Kurus had appointed to ascertain the conduct of his subjects toward the protection of prosperity,
arrived at the Dvaitavana forest as a forest-dweller, disguised in the garb of an ascetic, and was recognized by Yudhiṣṭhira.

When he had prostrated himself before the king and was about to announce that the earth had been conquered by his rival, his mind did not waver; for those who desire one's welfare do not wish to speak what is pleasant if it be false.

Desiring to bring about the destruction of his enemies, he obtained the king’s secret permission and uttered these words, which were characterized by excellence and nobility and whose meaning was firmly resolved: dviṣāṃ vighātāya vidhātum icchato rahasy anujñām adhigamya bhūbhṛtaḥ / sa sauṣṭhavaudāryaviśeṣaśālinīṃ viniścitārthām iti vācam ādadhe // BhKir_1.3 //
O King, those who possess spies for their eyes must not be deceived by their dependents while engaged in their duties;
therefore, you ought to forgive me whether my words be ill-spoken or well-spoken, for speech that is both beneficial and pleasing to the mind is rare.

What kind of friend is he who does not advise his lord what is beneficial? What kind of master is he who does not listen to [his ministers]? For all prosperity resides in kings and ministers who always take delight in those who are well-disposed toward them.
Where is the conduct of kings, which is by nature difficult to comprehend, and where are [ordinary] creatures, who are bewildered by ignorance?
It is only through your power that I have understood this path of policy of my enemies, whose true nature is so hidden.
Fearing defeat at the hands of you who dwell in the forest, Suyodhana— even while seated upon the royal throne— seeks to conquer the earth through policy, having won it by the ruse of dice.
Nevertheless, that crooked man spreads forth brilliant fame through the excellence of his virtues, desiring to conquer you;
for even enmity with great souls is better than associating with the ignoble while elevating one's prosperity.

Having conquered the group of six internal enemies and desiring to attain the human state that is otherwise inaccessible, he— free from sloth and dividing his time between night and day— exerts his manly effort through that method of policy.

Free from pride, he constantly shows affection to his dependents as if they were friends, treats his equals with honor, and regards his kinsmen as true companions, as if their kinship were a sovereignty already established.
As he served them appropriately according to their respective needs with impartial devotion,
the three groups— acting as if they had entered into friendship through their affection for his virtues— did not obstruct one another.
His conciliation was free from guile and never devoid of gifts; his abundant giving was never separated from respectful treatment.
His conduct, distinguished by excellence, proceeded in accordance with virtue, for such respectful treatment never occurs without regard for virtue.
Desiring neither wealth nor power, and not out of anger, but solely because it was his own duty, he ceased all other motives;
and whether against an enemy or even a son, he struck with punishment according to the instruction of his guru to suppress any violation of dharma.
Having provided protection for his enemies on all sides, he approaches them with an appearance free from suspicion, though he himself is suspicious;
his subjects declare that his prosperity demonstrates his gratitude toward those who have been made his dependents during the completion of his undertakings.
By him, the means of attainment— having been properly analyzed and honored with correct application—
were made to yield results incessantly, like abundant stores of wealth that, having entered into competition, bring forth prosperity for the future.

The ichor of the elephants presented as gifts by kings— possessing a fragrance like that of the *ayugmachhada* flower— drenches to excess the courtyard of his assembly hall, which is crowded with the chariots, horses, and men of many monarchs.

In that land, the Kurus shine for a long time, extending security and prosperity; there, the abundance of crops is obtained with ease by the farmers, as if ripening without being ploughed, and the people are not dependent on rain-gods for their sustenance.
Possessing great vigor, with honor as their wealth, honored for their riches, and bearing bows, these warriors have won renown in battle;
neither united nor acting with dissension, they desire to achieve what is pleasing to him even at the cost of their lives.
The earth, milked by his own virtues, yielded treasures for him who was like Vasu— of noble fame, compassionate, and providing protection that dispelled all affliction.
Having completed all his own duties, he learned through his spies—the very conduct of kings—without leaving anything undone;
for the intentions of that king were understood through his great successes which resulted in beneficial consequences, just as the purpose of a deity is inferred from its fruits.
Never has he raised a strung bow anywhere, nor has he made his face crooked with anger;
rather, out of affection for his virtues, kings carry his command upon their heads like a garland.
Having installed Duḥśāsana, arrogant in his fresh youth, in the position of crown prince, that king of powerful commands—
unwearied in sacrifices and approved by his family priest— propitiates the Fire-god with oblations.

Although he rules the circle of the earth as far as the oceans, with its kings already subdued and his dominion enduring, he still dwells in constant anxiety regarding the fears that will come from you; alas, enmity with the powerful leads to endless calamity!
When his prowess as the son of Indra is recalled by people in the course of conversation,
he, with face bowed down, suffers at the mention of your name like a serpent at the sound of unbearable words of a mantra.
Therefore, while you are prepared to act swiftly with deceit, let the appropriate countermeasure be taken;
for those like me, whose intellects consist essentially of worldly activity, must indeed gather the words uttered by others.
Having spoken these words, when her husband, who had received due honors from the forest-dwellers, had departed,
Kṛṣṇā entered the king’s residence and related those words in the presence of his younger brothers.
Having heard of the success of her enemies and their subsequent removals from power, the daughter of Drupada— unable to restrain herself— uttered words that inflamed the king’s wrath and resolve.
To those such as you, the speech of women is like an insult rather than an instruction;
nevertheless, my heavy sorrows—which cast aside all the conventions of womankind—compel me to speak.
This earth, held for a long time without interruption by kings born of your own lineage whose splendor equaled that of Indra,
has been surrendered by you with your own hand, like a garland cast off by a rutting elephant.
Those of deluded intellect meet with defeat who do not employ guile against those who are deceitful;
for such rogues, having entered [them], destroy them—just as sharp arrows strike down those whose limbs are unshielded.

O lord of men, what other than you—being devoted to virtue, possessing loyal means, and proud of his lineage—could deprive one of such fortune, who is as dear to her as a wife, for she is attached to him through her virtues and born of a noble family?
Like one's own beautiful bride, who else but you could take away such prosperity from another?
O god among men, as you now turn away from the path censured by the wise,
how is it that your rising indignation does not blaze forth like a high-flaming fire against a dry śamī tree?
Embodied beings submit of their own accord to one whose anger is never in vain and who destroys calamities;
yet a person who is devoid of indignation, lacking both affection and resentment toward others, does not command the respect of people.
Wandering on foot through the mountains, accustomed to red sandalwood paste yet now covered in dust,
does this Vṛkodara— who was once a great chariot-warrior— perhaps distress your mind, O you whose wealth is truth?
How is it that Dhanañjaya, who— resembling Indra— conquered the prosperous Northern Kurus and bestowed upon you untold wealth,
now feels no indignation while stripping you of your bark garments?
With forms hardened by their beds at the edge of the forest, their bodies covered in matted hair like two elephants from the Himālayas,
how is it that you do not strive to overcome these twin sons of Yama, who possess such fortitude and self-restraint?
I know this thought of yours to be not your own; indeed, the fluctuations of the mind take on manifold forms.
As I contemplate your supreme distress, these mental agonies violently pierce my heart.
You who were formerly awakened upon a costly couch with songs of praise and auspicious hymns,
now lie upon a ground strewn with abundant darbha grass and abandon sleep to the inauspicious howls of jackals.

O King, that beauty which was previously brought forth by this food remaining from the twice-born has now reached its utmost emaciation— your body, along with your fame, as you subsist on forest fruits.
Those two feet of yours, which have never ceased to delight with the dust from the crests of royal crowns as they rest upon jeweled pedestals—
now let them rest in the forests upon the sacrificial grass whose tips have been nibbled by deer and birds.
Since this condition is caused by an enemy, it seems to uproot my very mind from its foundation;
for to those who possess an unassailable excellence of valor, even defeat at the hands of others is nothing but a festival.
O King, having abandoned that abode of peace, be gracious once more and engage in battle for the destruction of your enemies;
for it is sages who, free from desire, attain perfection through tranquility after casting off their foes, not kings.
If those like you— leaders of the illustrious, whose wealth is their fame— having encountered such unbearable insult,
should entrust themselves to others, then alas, noble-mindedness is destroyed when left without support.
Now, if you seek for yourself the means to happiness through forbearance alone, having long since cast aside all other instruments,
then abandon the bow that bears the mark of the Lord of Fortune, and wearing matted locks, offer oblations here to the sacred fire.
It is not fitting for you, who possess such great majesty, to observe an agreement with enemies intent on deceit;
for kings seeking victory over their foes employ treacherous pacts as a means of corrupting them.

May Fortune attend you once again, like the sun at the beginning of the day after it has dispelled the darkness of its enemies— the sun which, due to the constraints of its appointed time, had become dim through the withdrawal of its radiance, its strength slackened, and was submerged in the fathomless ocean of calamity.
Then Vṛkodara, having ascertained that the speech uttered by his beloved was most weighty, pleasing to the mind, and supported by sound reasoning, addressed these words to the king: *BhKir_2.1*
That which the proud lady spoke, looking all around with eyes full of affection,
would cause even the Lord of Speech himself to wonder at such words so difficult to utter.
Even a difficult course of conduct is traversed when a way has been made, like a body of water with a constructed ford;
yet rare indeed is that person who, being virtuous, points out the path of duty in such circumstances.
When this speech, though painful to those whose vital strength is wounded, brings about a greater happiness in its ultimate result,
its virtue is seen to be great despite its brevity, like a most potent medicine that is small in quantity.
May these words, possessing radiant meaning and endowed with desirable qualities, be pleasing to you as well;
for the wise, in accepting a speech, are indeed indifferent to the particularity of the speaker and are guided solely by its merits.
O King, you have attained firm mastery in all four branches of knowledge that require discernment;
how then has your intellect fallen into error and become mired like an elephant in the mud?
What could be more calamitous than this— that even though you have been reduced to such a state, censured by enemies,
your manly prowess, which was once esteemed even by the gods, now sinks into despair?

For one of sound intellect who desires prosperity, the rise of enemies is better endured than their ultimate destruction; for even a great decline, if it tends toward the attainment of fruit, is preferable.
Having soon perceived that another’s prosperity is great while one’s own is the opposite, the wise man disregards the prospect of his own decline; otherwise, he takes remedial action against it.
While they fail to protect their rising sovereign power through inaction,
the fortunes of those kings depart before long, as if out of fear of public reproach.

Subjects bow to a king who, though subject to decay, maintains his innate auspicious luster for the sake of prosperity— an undiminishing sovereign who has risen like the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Indeed, policy (*naya*), which has determined its five constituent parts, is the source of both the treasury and the army;
it conforms to the necessity of skill regarding matters to be executed, just as the world conforms to destiny.
For a high-minded man possessed of self-respect who seeks to ascend to a lofty station,
his own manly effort is considered the proper support, capable of averting a downfall.
Calamities overcome one who lacks valor; prosperity abandons one who is beset by misfortune;
insignificance is certain for one without prosperity; and one who is not great does not attain the station of royal splendor.
Therefore, enough of resorting to despondency as an antidote for pride;
for prosperities that depend upon valor do not dwell together with despair.

Moreover, if a deadline is awaited, how can it be tolerated by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who has openly displayed his deceitful conduct after long enjoying the royal splendors that are so difficult to relinquish?
Or if you have recovered your own position through the efforts of your enemy, then,
O Lord of Men, the purpose of your younger brothers— whose manliness has been made manifest by their arms— has already been fulfilled.
The lord of beasts sustains himself with elephants slain by his own hand, their faces drenched in rut;
indeed, a great man, surpassing the world by his own splendor, does not seek prosperity from another.
For one whose wealth is pride and who seeks enduring fame through fleeting vital breaths,
prosperity— fickle as the play of a flash of lightning— is indeed but a secondary consequence.
People do not leap upon a heap of ashes covering a blazing fire;
therefore, out of fear of being overwhelmed, those who possess self-respect easily abandon their lives rather than their honor.
Considering what fruit does the lord of beasts seek from the thundering clouds?
For such is the very nature of the great that they cannot endure the rising of another.
O King, cast off the darkness born of negligence and direct your mind toward valor;
know this for certain: the calamities of your enemies will be destroyed by your lack of energy.
Who among enemies could withstand your younger brothers in battle— those who, like elephants renowned throughout the quarters, are as vast as the four oceans, and possess the splendor of Indra?
May the continuous stream of tears from the eyes of the wives of your enemies bring peace to your heart, O Jātavedas, as you blaze incessantly against them.
Thus, the lord of the earth proceeded to appease his son, who had displayed such agitation and whose mind was overcome with anger,
just as one would approach to soothe a rogue elephant.
In your pure, heart-captivating,
and auspicious discourse, which is free from error, your stainless intellect is clearly perceived as if in a mirror.
Clarity was not discarded by the words, nor was the weight of the meaning withheld;
the distinctness of the sense in each phrase was composed, and the inherent power of the expressions was nowhere set aside.
Rebirth has been established by the force of inference, and scripture is not contradicted;
what person with a mind other than this would venture to speak so forcefully against it?
Nevertheless, because of my lack of satiety, my heart still rushes toward certainty;
for the excellence of specific qualities found among those subject to destiny is not sufficient to bring about final resolution.
One should not perform an action impulsively; lack of discernment is the ultimate seat of calamities.
For prosperity, being attracted by virtue, seeks out the one who acts with deliberation of its own accord.
He who, guarding the seeds of ritual according to rule, rains upon them with the water of solitude,
ever presides over an action rich in fruit, like the autumn season over the world.
Learning adorns a pure body, and tranquility is its ornament;
valor is the adornment of tranquility, and it is further adorned by success achieved through prudent policy.
When the path of action for the discerning is obscured by the darkness of conflicting opinions and is thus profound,
the well-established and pure tradition provides a vision of the goal, like a lamp.
For those who fix their minds on the path trodden by great-souled ones whose virtues are worthy of longing,
even a downfall— though caused by fate and not by sin— is equal to success.
Having calculated what is auspicious, appropriate, conducive to the greatest accomplishment of results, and free from harm to the future,
those who desire victory direct their human effort, having conquered the impulse of anger.
One who desires to dispel the darkness consisting of anger rising before them must do so with their intellect;
for even the sun does not rise by its mere radiance unless it first pierces through the darkness created by night.
He who does not ward off the onset of the darkness born of anger, even though he be powerful,
destroys all his stores of strength, just as the waning fortnight destroys the digits of the moon.
That lord of the earth who maintains impartiality, yet displays gentleness at the proper time and extends severity when necessary,
presides over the world with his splendor like the sun.
Where is the long-term possession of riches, and where is the state of being subject to the horses of the wicked senses?
For riches, flickering like autumn clouds, are difficult for those with unsteady senses to guard and are full of deception.
Why do you, by causing an untimely agitation of your mind which has already acquired such momentum,
act as the master of the waters, having surpassed even the Ocean in steadfastness?
Those who, even after attaining sacred learning, do not subdue the enemies born of their own bodies,
truly bring about the swift ruin of their prosperity through the disgrace inherent in their restlessness.
Impatience, which causes one to miss the proper time for action and brings torment to one's own body and senses,
ought not— like the conduct of common folk— to deprive you of the attainment of the right method.
There is no means equal to forbearance (titikṣā) for securing a great future benefit, for the abundant ripening of the fruits of action,
nor for the unfailing destruction of enemies.

Setting us aside, who are ever inclined toward prostration with hearts bound by natural affection, the Vṛṣṇis do not bow to Suyodhana; for among those who possess self-respect, he is not the first to whom they should bow.
Those friends— whether born with him, natural, or otherwise— who do not transgress his will,
conduct themselves toward the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as if out of discipline for their own spiritual attainment.
Therefore, you must launch an attack against these kings once that deadline has passed;
he will shatter them as the sun, rising up, opens the beds of lotuses.

Transgressing those kings who were susceptible to subversion, that creator of discord, arrogant with pride, did not tolerate even the humiliation of common people— how much less so the royal assembly, which possesses a splendor superior to the world?
For those who possess pride, even a modest degree of success in their undertakings— though their momentum has been checked by discipline—
is sufficient to cause their prosperity to swell with arrogance.
Folly invariably does not part from a king who is arrogant with pride;
the excessively foolish is cast out from statesmanship, and from one devoid of statesmanship, the people turn away in resentment.

Like a tree, even a great enemy— though its roots may be extensive— is easy for a patient man to uproot, provided he is stirred by the wind of disaffection and gradually causes the continuity of its foundations to decay.
Even a slight internal conflict arising from the provocation of subjects destroys a sovereign;
for fire produced by the friction of the tips of tree branches utterly consumes even a mountain.
A wise man should remain indifferent toward the rising power of an enemy who destroys discipline;
for such an enemy is easily conquered when he is in his internal state of ruin, for prosperity that lacks discipline ends in calamity.

The immediate enemy, having overwhelmed the king’s circle of vassals— which has become divided both outwardly and inwardly due to its weak conduct— strips it away, just as the force of a river erodes a crumbling bank.

The son of Parāśara approached that elder brother of Arjuna— who was instructing him with an unconfused mind upon the path of policy, which is otherwise so perplexing— just as a desired object approaches one of its own accord.
Even toward animals, he brought about tranquility with his sweet glances;
he bore everywhere a powerful radiance capable of being beheld, which was the very fire that consumes all sins.
Suddenly approached with wonder, that sage— the progenitor of asceticisms and the non-progenitor of sins—
was beheld by the lord of the earth like an embodied accumulation of merit.
Then, rising from his most excellent seat with the tips of his shaken, reddish-brown bark garments fluttering,
he shone like the sun upon the peak of Sumeru, its web of rays scattered in a golden glow.
With a concentrated mind, having performed the worthy rites as prescribed by his teacher for the most eminent of sages like a seer himself,
the king subsequently graced the seat with his presence, just as tranquility adorns sacred learning.
With his lips illuminated by the rays of a smile clearly manifest, standing facing the Sage whose splendor was diffused,
he bore the beauty of the entire moon-like form as it extended a blazing web of rays toward its preceptor on all sides.

Then [he saw him] bearing matted locks of tawny hue, dark-blue in luster, like a cloud accompanied by lightning, with upward-reaching networks of rays as beautiful as the autumn moonbeams that made him appear as if tall.
Bearing the full splendor of grace through his preeminent physical form that transcends all people,
he forcibly instills a moist affection even in the hearts of those who were strangers.
He was extending a state of inner composure that was free from agitation;
it was as if he had already engaged in conversation with his gaze, which possessed a particular sweetness and confidence.
The son of Dharma, desiring to know the cause of that sage’s arrival— the source of the scriptures that bind one to righteousness and dispel sin— addressed the sage as he sat comfortably.
This attainment of seeing you, which is difficult to reach through the mere accumulation of unearned merit and which brings forth the fruit that has shaken off all dust,
is equal to a rain from the heavens when the clouds have vanished.
Today, rituals have become like cows of plenty, and the priests' blessings have become true;
for since you arrived, O God upon Earth, I have been born among the worlds as one worthy of great honor until the end of this cycle of existence.
It draws forth prosperity, destroys evils, bathes one in excellence, and spreads renown;
what does this unfailing sight of the Teacher of the World not bestow, as if it were the sight of the Self-born Creator himself?
Even before the moon with its dripping rays, my eye finds no peace;
yet in your presence, having cast off the sorrow of separation from kinsmen, my heart seems to breathe again.
A curiosity regarding questions directed toward us is groundless, for what can we offer those who are free from desire?
Nevertheless, my desire to hear your speech, which brings about such auspiciousness, makes me eloquent.
Having spoken thus, the king— whose mind was fixed on the attainment of victory and who delighted in such refined speech—
being noble-minded, addressed these noble words to Dvaipāyana.
For those who desire to attain a great prosperity, adorned with fame, in both worlds,
a conduct that is equally respectful toward kinsmen is especially appropriate for those whose wealth is their asceticism.
Nevertheless, O King, my heart has been subdued by the flood of your virtues and made humble;
for even those who are free from desire and partakers of liberation feel partiality toward the worthy.
Are you not the daughters of that king, or have you not surpassed Suyodhana in virtues?
That he has abandoned you—whether out of folly or by force—is merely the delusion of one who lusts after sensual objects.
How could he not abandon this man, who stands among Karṇa and others while his success is still in doubt?
For obstacles to victory arising from ill-timed efforts are the very footsteps of calamities that crush one's fortune.
By you, who for a long time have borne the burden of righteousness even when the assembly of enemies had strayed from the path,
supreme love for virtues has been revealed as something beautiful that remains undisturbed even in times of adversity.
Having brought about your own destruction through a stratagem against you— who were devoted solely to tranquility—
your enemies have revealed the essence of your wisdom and virtue, as if they had rendered you a service.
The earth can be won by your prowess, for your adversary is superior in terms of heroism, weapons, and strength;
therefore, a plan for further excellence must be devised, for in battle, the glory of victory depends upon preeminence.
The son of Jamadagni, the preceptor who was the slayer of the lords of the earth twenty-one times, then realized that his own prowess had been surpassed;
he understood that excellence in virtues depends upon the capacity of their receptacle.
Before whom even Antaka, though he has suffered the pain of losing his sovereignty and as if having met with defeat,
trembles while brandishing his bow— who would not have his mind inclined solely toward fear in battle before that Bhīṣma?
Who could withstand you in battle as you discharge volleys of arrows, like a heavy fire blazing with rage,
with tongues of flickering, trembling flames at their tips, as if wishing to devour the entire world?
Beholding the son of Rādhā, whose fortitude had been cast aside by his fury and who had propitiated Jamadagni,
even Death himself might feel partiality toward him in the midst of unprecedented terrors.
By means of this [bow], which was acquired as the instrument for performing most difficult ascetic penance,
these [beings]— having attained power that is hard to obtain— were made to blossom by the one who bears the ape-banner.

O King, worthy of receiving gifts, I have come to you as if to a perfected lore (*siddhi*)— a lore of vast splendor, capable of bestowing the attainment of greatness upon those of great majesty, and worthy of being propitiated by the gods themselves.
When he had spoken thus, Arjuna, honoring the words of Ajātaśatru,
approached him who was gracious, as one dwelling nearby might do with humility, saying, "Go, accomplish your purpose."

Then, like the light of the sun emerging from its orb at the dawn of day, that radiance— white as sparks of fire— issued forth from the mouth of the great seer and entered the face of Pārtha, like a shimmering lotus.
And by the power of his asceticism, he immediately bestowed that yoga upon him who was most worthy of it, whereby,
once the light of reality had been produced within him, his eye— as it were— finally opened after a long time.
Perceiving that he bore an appearance foretelling abundant gain and was inwardly disposed according to his heart's desire,
the sage, wishing to enjoin him to the practice of austerity for the sake of attaining victory, spoke as follows.
His splendor increased through this yoga;
not yielding his own station to another, he practiced the conduct of sages, bearing his weapons, by means of recitation, fasting, and ritual ablutions.
Where you shall perform austerities most difficult to practice for the sake of propitiating the Destroyer of the Mountain-clan (Śiva),
this Guhyaka shall lead you in an instant to that mountain-mass of lovely peaks.
As the great seer was speaking thus to the son of Mahendra, he vanished;
yet the attendant of the king of kings remained visibly present in his vicinity, like an instruction firmly established in his mind.
Having bowed down when addressed with words of consolation, that holy man conceived a longing for Jishnu;
he attained a state of serene confidence as if toward a friend, for the union of the virtuous inspires trust quickly.
Then, as the sun causes the groves of Mount Sumeru to fade at its rising,
so did darkness— having gained strength through that [sorrow] and causing great pain— gradually seize the sons of Pāṇḍu, who were once possessed of great splendor.
Driven by the performance of his duty without hesitation, and being brought together and shared out through love,
even that excessive burden of suffering was felt as light by their minds, as if from an equal distribution.
Due to the steadfastness and trustworthiness of the great seer, and because of the intense wrath arising from his enemy,
as well as the prowess of Maghavan’s son known among the wise, grief found no footing among them.
Leaving far behind those four regions of abundant splendor, as if they were the watches of the day,
that mass of misfortune fell upon Kṛṣṇā like darkness upon the night.

Fearing the destruction of her auspiciousness, she was unable to close her eyes when looking at him— even though her inner feelings were not concealed— though they resembled blue lotuses covered by a film of frost and were filled with tears.

The son of Indra received with the cupped hands of his delighted mind that gaze of Rāma, which was charming with the flavor of unfeigned affection, bestowed upon him, and enchanting to behold— receiving it as if it were the provisions for his journey.
Her serenity stolen by the collapse of her fortitude, like a summer river by a wild elephant, the princess spoke with difficulty, her voice choked and the flow of her tears suppressed: BhKir_3.38.
As if intending to extract the great prosperity of all beings from the mire of the enemy's deceit,
do not become excessively despondent on my account before the success of your austerities against your foes has been achieved.

Success, as if longing for them, comes to the lap of those who are free from desire yet engaged in effort— whether to attain fame, to seek pleasure, or even to transcend the mere status of being counted among men.
Stealing away the victorious wealth and vigor of the Kṣatriyas— ordained by the Creator to protect the world—
he struck down their pride, which was their sole means of victory and as dear to them as life itself.
Brought by his trusted attendants while bowing in shame, he was received with difficulty by the kings who hesitated;
he seemed to gather together his fame, which had spread across the earth like a canopy and was scattered throughout the quarters.
Having shown no despondency in his heroic exploits, he spread a semblance of non-existence,
like the remnant of the sun’s rays at the end of the day, which, while exhausting its power for the future, creates the impression that it has ceased to be.
This humiliation, which others have forcibly inflicted upon us—something impossible even to remember, let alone to remedy—is like fresh moisture drying up; without you, it will wither my heart.
Due to the calamity of his pride, he has fallen into an unbearable state of transformation, like an elephant suffering from the affliction of its tusks;
his great splendor eclipsed by the majesty of the enemy, he is like the morning sun obscured by autumnal clouds.
Because of his inactivity, you do not shine with your weapons as much as before, appearing as if they were blunted by shame;
like an ocean whose waters have been exhausted by the destruction of its fame, you seem to have assumed a different form.

With these locks of hair, scattered by the dust of Duḥśāsana’s indignation, which have become like luckless men deprived of their wealth, has the very essence of your prowess been rendered useless? Are you indeed that same Dhanañjaya?
That Kṣatriya is capable of protecting the virtuous—he whose power lies in his bow for deeds;
yet, if he bears this twofold [duty] toward a fruitless end, he makes his speech as if it were devoid of refinement.
O Pārtha, your virtues— deprived of their luster and reduced to mere existence— emulate your likeness as if sharing your sorrow, for they look only toward the prosperity you have brought about.

Just as the splendor of day mounts the sun by its brilliance, so this burden, through its fitness, has mounted you— who, through negligence, were being dragged away by enemies like a lion with unshorn manes by serpents.
He who, through his deeds, makes his reputation— surpassing that of all other people— meaningful,
such that when the status of a superior man arises in assemblies, the number "one" does not merely serve as a filler for him.

O Pārtha, may Maghavan bring about the destruction of those sins by which your mind becomes weary when contemplating beloved things that cannot be attained— sins that shall befall you as you set forth for victory.
Do not, wandering alone for long, fall into negligence even while dwelling in a place that is unconfined and auspicious;
for the minds of those whose souls are afflicted by envy and passion falter even toward the virtuous.
Therefore, quickly carrying out the word of the great seer, make our heart's desires bear fruit;
for when you have returned having accomplished your purpose, I long to embrace you closely, pressing my breasts against you.
Upon hearing those words spoken by Yājñasenī— which revived and intensified her grievances— he blazed forth intensely, like the sun reaching its northern course.

Then, as if beholding his enemies before him, he had a multitude of weapons placed upon him by his domestic priest; though naturally charming, he assumed a terrifying form, like a mantra employed for malevolent sorcery.
A bow whose string was famous for its sound and which could not be drawn by enemies; two great quivers equipped with sharp swords, yet remaining out of the range of the enemy's sight.
Repeatedly concealing the wounds from the weapons of the mountain-shatterer with his own splendor as if with fame,
and wearing his gem-studded armor, he appeared like the interior of the sky filled with blazing light.
Traveling along the path of the mountain, which was shown by the servants of the Lord of the Unmanifest,
that ascetic entered for a moment the hearts of those whose eyes were filled with tears.
Then the quarters of the sky followed with the divine sound of kettledrums, and the splendor of the heavens was spread by the falling of celestial flowers;
the ocean, its arms in the form of restless waves at the shore, embraced the quivering earth as if to tell her something dear.

Then he, beloved of the people, approached the region of Upajana, which had a girdle of warbling swans and possessed the quality of a pale hue bestowed by ripening crops, just as one approaches a beloved woman who has attained her youth.

Beholding the lands along the borders, which were graced by the abundance of bending rice stalks, whose waters were free from mud and filled with lotuses, and which had become the very embodiment of the beauty and virtues of autumn, he rejoiced.
As if gazing with waters agitated by wonder, their lotus-eyes opened wide,
the darting movements of the fish captivated his mind, stealing away the playful charms of the glances of his beloved.
He was filled with delight beholding the exceeding beauty of the water of the Kālmasī river, together with its lotuses;
for who would not rejoice in the excellence of a rare union with a worthy mate?
He dispelled his doubt regarding the land-lotuses— doubts manifested as a succession of foam—
by the water which had reached the separation of its filaments and was violently struck by a rolling pāṭhīna fish.

Having observed the ocean’s shore, where the waves had left their traces and the sand— pale as bleached silk— was being slowly smoothed by the waters whose flow had gradually subsided, he took delight in the lady of the sea.
Her charming space between the eyebrows was adorned with particles of saffron pollen;
with the beauty of her sprout-like lower lip, copper-red from lac-dye, she seemed to be equaling the *bandhujīvaka* flower.

She was radiant with the pollen of lotuses, her two breasts— like great mounds— reddened by fresh sunlight and repeatedly moistened on all sides by the sweat of exertion, which spread along with a thrill of horripilation.

Beholding the cowherd woman— who adorned the blue lotus of her ear-ornament with the luster of her eyes clinging to her cheek— the autumn season considered its purpose fulfilled through the son of Pāṇḍu.
Having ceased from their grazing in the late-night pastures and unable to run swiftly to their stalls,
the herds of cows— eager for him and with the milk flowing from their full udders— longed to gaze upon him who was eager to look at them.
He beheld the bull, surrounded by the glory of victory, bellowing loudly as he shattered the banks of the Sindhu river;
possessing autumnal vigor, he appeared like the personified pride of the cattle themselves.
Even as herds of cows, white as masses of snow, slowly released themselves,
they created a sense of wonder upon the autumn riverbanks with their slipping dewlaps, as if those were female hips clad in falling silk garments.

The son of Pāṇḍu beheld the cowherds in the forests, who had attained a natural kinship with the cattle and maintained a love for their homes; they seemed like imitations of cows themselves in their straightforwardness.
He wandered about with faces beautiful as lotuses brushed by the morning sun, crowded with bees that were his hair, displaying the filaments of teeth revealed by smiles,
and adorned by the radiance of swaying earrings.
With their lower lips trembling from suppressed sighs like creepers with a single quivering leaf,
they were drawn forward by the dragging of their hands— hands whose movements were captivating— as their sides were pushed back and their triple-jointed backs were bent.
In the courtyards of the cow-pens, the peacocks—suspecting the roar of clouds—were maddening their mates;
meanwhile, the jars, repeatedly tossed by the churning of the milk-seas, resounded as slowly as drums.
He did not cease gazing upon the cowherd women, whose full breasts trembled with their slow movements and whose lotus-eyes were weary from fatigue, appearing like courtesans who had begun to dance.
He descended to the roads that had abandoned their former crookedness, where the abundance of crops near the edges had been consumed by bulls,
where the thick mud was furrowed by the rims of chariot wheels, and which were divided apart by the continuous trampling of his followers.

He beheld the rows of houses, which resembled the pavilions of hermitages, surrounded by villagers of irreproachable conduct whose ornaments were their modest gestures, and which were smiling with blossoming flowers.

Then, beholding the splendor of the qualities of autumn, the Yakṣa spoke to him whose eyes were restless with the sight of those autumnal charms; for one who understands gestures does not fail to speak on a suitable occasion, even if unbidden.

May this autumn—whose waters are clear and who is free from rain-bearing clouds—augment your glory of victory, O Pārtha; for like the future course of Śiva’s destiny, she brings fulfillment to the world’s actions through their fruits.
The beauty of the ripening harvest approaches; the rivers attain a lack of turbulence; the earth achieves freedom from mud.
Now, through these new qualities, the love for the splendor of the rainy season—long established through familiarity—is eclipsed.
Neither do clear-winged birds alight upon it, nor do rows of clouds bearing the rainbow;
nevertheless, the sky nourishes a supreme beauty, for that which is naturally lovely does not depend on acquired qualities.
With breasts pale from illness and the golden threads of fresh lightning-garlands fallen away,
this emaciation of the quarter-women does not fail to shine at the departure of the wind-bearer of the Kadamba flowers.

Having abandoned its desire for the cry of the peacock that has arisen from the onset of intoxication because its throat is not reddened, the ear takes refuge in the sound of the intoxicated swan; for qualities are what authorize one's dearness, not mere acquaintance.
These rice plants, supporting broad stalks and turned tawny by the ripening of their grain,
bow down over the blooming water of the embankment as if to smell the blue lotus, its presence betrayed by its fragrance.
The water, colored by the luster of lotus-stalks, distinguished by the beauty of lotus petals,
and reddened by the tips of shimmering rice stalks, flowed swiftly like a fragment of Indra’s bow.
The women that were the forest rows, with their flower-smiles and eyes like unclouded arrows, checked the pale pollen of the *saptaparṇa* trees raised by the wind as if it were a thin, white garment.

The path of the sky was auspicious, its interior cooled by lotus-breezes carrying sprays of water from within; it was unlit by the fire born of lightning, yet its heat was obscured by the breaking apart of white clouds.

The pure quarters of the sky, emerging from the obstruction of the clouds, seem to engage in conversation with one another through the cries of these birds as they fly about, calling out to their white-winged mates.
Eager for the sound from the monastery grounds, the herds of cows have dropped their ranks;
these cows let their milk flow unceasingly from their udders, as if they were bringing offerings.
The source of the world, the sole purifier of the universe, having approached the vicinity of Vraja with her offspring,
this assembly of cows attains its full splendor, like a sacrificial oblation accompanied by mantras when combined with the *saṃhitā* texts.
Having fixed its attention on the sound of the songs of the cowherd women— more charming than the cries of peacocks—
the herd of does, abandoning its great desire to eat, no longer approaches the grain.
Disregarded by the lotus pond with utter indifference, though bowing his head, this paddy plant,
withering away along with the water, turns pale as if scorched by the god of love.
Stirred up by the wind that carries the pollen of lotuses or the drops of spray,
these bees are unable to determine their course, just as those who have committed evil deeds are unable to discern their destination when calamities approach.
Bearing the tawny crests of the *kalama* rice with beaks as red as fragments of coral,
this row of parrots, tender as a *śirīṣa* flower, follows the splendor of the bow of the Slayer of Mountains.
While he was speaking thus, not far away, the king of mountains appeared with the orb of the sun obscured by it,
like a mass of clouds white with the weight of falling water.
Having reached that mountain, whose lower slopes were darkened by rows of dense forests and which was white with masses of snow above,
the victorious Arjuna recalled the splendor of the plow-wielding Balarāma, who, his passion having subsided, wore a dark garment upon his lower lip.
Then he set out toward the lofty Himalaya, as if to conquer Mount Meru, or out of an impetuous desire to see the ends of the earth, or perhaps to leap across the sky that had risen up before him.
On one side illuminated by the orb of the sun, and on the other perpetually shrouded in nocturnal darkness,
it appeared like Śiva before him, followed by his elephant hide which dispels the mass of gloom with its laughter-like whiteness.
Dwelling upon the earth, in the sky, and in the world of the gods, they had built their homes without ever seeing one another;
it was as if Śambhu had created this representative to manifest his omnipresence throughout the worlds.
With its peaks resplendent with streaks of gold, the mountain— white as the king of serpents and possessing the splendor of the sky—
rose up like a mass of lightning-charged clouds that surpassed the gathering of autumnal rain-clouds.
The lands, radiant with the silken garments of the massed rays of jewels, containing bower-houses of creepers enjoyed by celestial nymphs,
and possessing gate-towers formed by lofty crags, appeared like cities with flowering groves arisen within them.
With clouds that were pale from discharging water incessantly and devoid of the brilliance of lightning,
and which hung over their broad hips with a low rumbling sound, the mountain appeared as if it had sprouted wings.

Behold the swift rivers, whose waters are honored and beneficial for various desires, possessing banks that are uneven yet level with their descents, scarred by elephants who have taken [their water] as if they were mines.

In some places, upon ridges with walls of piled gold, the mountain shone as if it were filled with the rays of the evening twilight by means of a mass of radiant great gems possessing the luster of freshly blossomed hibiscus flowers.
It was adorned by clusters of broad kadamba flowers, filled with groves of mālatī and tamāla trees,
sprinkled with light frost and dewy water, and possessed elephants with ever-flowing temporal secretions.
They saw no mountain peaks bereft of heaps of jewels, no mountain caves devoid of fruit-bearing trees,
no river-brides lacking broad lotuses, and no trees without flowers.
The ocean, its waters agitated by the heavy hips of the celestial damsels moving slowly without waistbands,
was surrounded on all sides by the hoods of the serpents, which were spread out and covered with clusters of lovely, creeper-like Bakula flowers that delighted their beloveds.

It bore a multitude of clouds, white as snow and pure from the absence of dust, held motionless by its peaks which were bright with the luster of many jewels; and the gathering of these rain-clouds was signaled by their thundering.
The lake Mānasa, pure and filled with flocks of swans, bore blooming lotuses;
and Śiva, whose mind was pure and who was accompanied by his entire host, was likewise filled with joy upon seeing him together with the daughter of the mountain.
With the fire born of medicinal herbs blazing all around the sky and the hosts of planetary chariots,
it repeatedly reminded the attendants of Śiva of the burning of Tripura night after night.
With its waters rising high, turning back against the obstruction of rocks, and scattering masses of spray,
the mountain bore the Ganges— uplifted upon its lofty ridges— as if she were holding a white fly-whisk.

Then, his mind filled with wonder at the sight of the mountain, he was addressed with affectionate words by the attendant of the Lord of Wealth; for eloquence indeed shines forth when there is an occasion for it.
Behold, this lord of mountains has appeared, suddenly capable of destroying the mass of evils of living beings,
as he makes the sky appear as if split a thousandfold with his peaks white as snow.
In this world, they constantly describe the inner state as something extremely difficult to attain and hard to cross over by means of scriptures that are themselves hard to master;
yet the Lotus-born One knows this supreme realm, which is like a vast forest pervading the directions, just as he knows the Supreme Person.
With bowers of creepers adorned with lovely shoots and flowers, and with masses of water graced by lotuses,
this [place] constantly excites longing even in women who possess self-control, despite being near their lovers.

Constantly filled with these riches— which are easily obtained by the most excellent and prudent leaders, as well as by the lords of the Guhyakas and the treasures— the earth shines, surpassing all other worlds.
I believe that this entire world, even the three worlds together, cannot equal this mountain, the father of Gaurī;
for the Lord of Bhavānī, whose glory is unknown to common folk, dwells upon it forever.
For those who desire to attain the supreme, pure state of Brahman, free from birth and old age,
thoughts that sever worldly existence arise from this [place] as if from a scripture that dispels darkness.

In this place, the couches— marked by the lac-dye from the feet of celestial women, strewn with heaps of flowers that have fallen during their passion, and covered with blossoms that bear the traces of their embrace— proclaim with hope the excellence of the amorous delights enjoyed here.
In this world, when a lord of the earth— who is endowed with excellence of virtue, has attained supreme greatness,
and is possessed of statesmanship— is thus honored, the medicinal herbs do not cease their blazing, as if they were the goddess Śrī herself.
The flocks of ospreys have raised their cries; the trees are bent with blossoms; here the lotus ponds are filled with lotuses;
and the rivers, lined with *varaṇa* trees and *nalada* grass, provide delight for the elephants.
Bearing a fragrance produced by the sprinkling of rut-fluid that has acquired a resemblance to the scent of blossoming mangoes,
the rubbing of the temples of the celestial elephants, with bees clinging to it, intoxicates the cuckoos out of season.

This mountain, ancient with its forests, beautiful with its slopes, and long surrounded by rivers resonant with pleasant sounds— this very place, protected and abounding in fruits, where the earth has been stripped of all else and only the essence remains, dwells as if it were nectar itself.
In this place, the beautiful creepers are the dwelling, the medicinal herbs are the lamps, and the fresh sprouts of yellow sandalwood are the bed;
here, the breezes from the lotuses dispel the fatigue of love’s play, and thus they do not cause the celestial beauties to long for heaven.
There, while she was performing austerities for a long time in the water for the sake of Īśa, her eyes restless as they leaped over the aquatic creatures,
Bhava seized the hand of Bhavānī with his own hand, from whose fingers the sweat of the summer heat trickled down.

That very Mount Mandara, by which the ocean was churned for the nectar by gods and asuras— its waters cast aside and its serpent-dwellings shattered— now shines as if scraping the sky with its revolutions, marked by the coils of the lord of serpents.
Repeatedly raised by the rays of the hot-rayed sun, and displaying a heightened luster through gems of a dark-blue hue,
the shadow cast upon walls of crystal and silver— pale as a swan or a hawk— induces the suspicion that it is moonlight even in the middle of the day.
In these waters, which are as curved as the movement of the eyebrows of graceful, playful women, the lotuses— shaken by the gently falling breeze— are performing a dance full of charm.
In this [ceremony], the hand of the Goddess— whose eyes were tremulous with fear and upon whom auspicious great herbs had been placed— was sportively grasped by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
whose own hand was adorned with a bracelet of sloughed-off serpents and trembling.
The mass of rays produced from pure jewels, scattered here by countless splendors that traverse the path of the clouds,
seems to transcend the number seven of the sun’s rays as it spreads throughout this world.

This is that very Kailāsa, upon which the Lord of Wealth built a city with lofty gate-towers for the delight of the conqueror of the cities; it causes the sun, as he approaches its vicinity, to set prematurely.
In the interior valleys and amidst the ridges, covered by the convergence of the lights of various jewels,
the wind repeatedly strikes down each wall-like formation it encounters, shattering the very suspicion that they were solid walls.
The lovely, fresh luster does not depart from the grassy meadows; the lotus groves grow ever darker day by day;
and in this place, the sprouts of the trees, laden with clusters of variegated blossoms, do not cease to flourish.
In the surrounding regions, deer have licked and then released these gems out of suspicion that they were sprouts of green grass;
here, the lusters of the jewels, tender as young parrots and mingled with the rays of the sun, shine forth.
The pollen born of lotuses, wafted from that grove of full-blown land-lotuses and whirled about in the sky by the winds, assumes everywhere the splendor of a golden parasol.

Here, at dawn, on the celestial river where both are observing vows, the uneven path marked by the lines of the left foot stained with lac tells of the union of the bodies of Śiva and Śivā during their amorous turns.
Here, the shimmering masses of rays from the sun, emerging through the lattice-work of branches from the light-trees and reflecting off the walls of silver,
repeatedly flash forth like circles of mirrors.
With his form enveloped by masses of white rays, his massive body rounded by the impact against the mountain ridges,
the bull of the Lord of Ganas occupies the peaks, causing the womenfolk to suspect him for the moon.
Now that the mass of clouds has gradually and with great difficulty attained its birth, becoming thin and depleted of water,
the rays of the crest-jewels possess the power here to fill the various fragments of Indra’s shattered bow.
With rays that drip drops of nectar and resemble the fresh sprouts of trees entwined with young creepers,
the crescent moon of Śambhu constantly purifies the forest edge here during the long dark nights.

This mountain, beloved by your father, whose many golden caverns are like those of a mountain of gold, scatters across the forest a vast, golden luster as if it were a wide-spreading, voluminous robe.
The rays of the sun, doubled by their reflections on the golden banks of the rivers there, suddenly strip away the clinging moisture from the creepers with their beams;
thus, they repeatedly mimic the flashes of lightning upon the shores.

Here, the passage of the celestial elephant is inferred by means of the yellow sandalwood trees, which have been driven away by great serpents at his mere touch, abandoned by rutting elephants who were momentarily intoxicated, and drenched with his ichor.
Here, because the mass of rays from the sun is obstructed by the thick nets of clouds and the brilliance of black stones,
the mountain’s glow— its caves unilluminated— appears as if it were enveloped in darkness.
Though you are capable through this teaching of the Sage, remain on the path of the warrior class and practice austerity with vigilance;
for generally, even when a beneficial course of action exists, it is difficult to attain prosperity without obstacles.
May your horses, the senses, not be led astray onto wrong paths; may Śiva grant you auspicious devotion during this period of fervor.
May the world-protectors, guarding your ascetic power, ensure that your life is spent in action that is both virtuous and highly fruitful.

Having spoken thus, when the servant of the King of Kings had departed for his own abode—having offered what was beneficial and pleasing to one worthy of such affection—the son of Pṛthā brooded with longing; for separation from the virtuous indeed brings forth intense despondency.
He approached that mountain— which was unsurpassable in every respect due to its connection with essential strength, which was endowed with manifold fruits marked by auspicious signs,
and which was not diminished— just as one of abundant fortune might approach his own manly effort long cherished in his heart.
Then the son of Indra ascended that mountain, which possessed a beautiful form like the supreme Person upon the golden-peaked [Meru],
the lord of all things that fly, and which held the true path as it embraced the triple-streamed river.
Like blameless bards, the trees— whose swaying, crooked crests were stirred by the wind and whose cries of victory were the humming of bees— honored him with flowers, as if he were the son of Indra.
The pleasant breezes, carrying particles of pollen from the *avadhūta* lotuses and breaking the waves of the slender waters of the Gaṅgā,
came before him and embraced him like dear friends embracing a friend.
The sounds of the waters, mingled with the splashing against rising stones and joined by the clear cries of swans and cranes,
spread throughout the riverbanks, surpassing the resonance of auspicious musical instruments.

Before him, amidst a mass of waters from the celestial river that had broken down the lofty trees of the gods, he beheld the humility practiced by the groves of reeds— a humility that brings prosperity when directed toward one who is more powerful.
He was unable to look all around at the flock of swans, which were reddened by the pollen of lotuses,
shimmering with waves, and appearing like a river’s upper garment gathered together.
Wounds were inflicted upon the riverbank by the flow of rut-fluid from the elephant that had been subdued, while the female bees there rejoiced;
yet he established even greater fortitude on that shore—for even when causing great pain, a great man serves a noble purpose.

He rejoiced in the piteous cries of the female cakravāka birds, which followed their male companions as they reached a state of equality with the broad, reddish waves that rivaled the hue of molten gold.
The rays of the white-horsed sun, skillful in weaving the hues of trembling waves,
appeared like forms conceived in the mind, shimmering even though the mass of jewels was submerged in the water.
He beheld the foam of the waters, white as the tip of a *ketaka* flower, borne by waves tossed upward by the impact and scattered by the swift, blowing wind— like the laughter of the river.
The river made a mass of the water of his gifts, resembling many peacock feathers,
into a hundred blooming eyes, as if to plunge deep and gaze upon the Lord of Elephants.
On the riverbank, a lotus-eyed woman beheld a pearl-oyster shell, its mouth opened wide by the yawning of awakening;
it appeared like a female oyster shedding teardrops, as clear pearls fell from within like falling drops of tears.
Pure in the water, its branches entwined with coral creepers and covered with dense fragments of foam,
it intensely reminded one of the beloved’s lower lip, which bestows passion and bears the luster of teeth.
And perceiving the scent of rut carried by the restless waves as they rose from the water,
he perceived the elephants facing him like rival tuskers.

He was filled with wonder as he beheld before him a mass of water, resembling an autumn cloud, which had been cast into the sky by the breaths of a serpent suddenly wishing to leap upward, and which moved with the speed of those swift winds.

He crossed the rivers flowing toward the celestial river, which possessed beautiful eyes in the form of shimmering fish upon their sandy banks and broad hips in the form of their lovely curves, appearing like charming female companions.

Having ascended, he reached a pure region at the edge of the forest upon the summit of the mountain— a place whose surface was adorned on all sides by trees whose tops were bent down under the weight of their blossoms— as if it were the very serenity of his own mind.
The mountain, with its ridges covered by spreading flowering creepers and its secluded forests filled with fruit-bearing great trees,
inspired steadfastness in Hari’s son to dwell upon that immovable peak for the sake of asceticism.
Having first resolved there according to the prescribed rite to assume the state of a sage, the ancient seer undertook an arduous penance;
for what austerity, however difficult, can cause despondency to those who possess self-mastery?

Subduing the darkness consisting of evil through pure virtues, he whose sole happiness was the tranquility of his restrained senses increased day by day with the virtuous, like the stainless moon with its digits.
And because he praised the quality of discernment, his mind turned away from the lack of virtue;
for him, who was free from affliction, the experience of the bliss of tranquility eclipsed the obstructive delight in attachment to sense objects.

Having approached the Lord of Heaven with mental recitations, prayers, and prostrations while remaining self-restrained, he simultaneously bore two splendors: one innate and the other consisting of victory and tranquility.
Bearing matted locks on his head, which resembled emeralds due to the water used for the consecration of the newborn,
he bore a resemblance to a *tamāla* tree whose crown is brushed by the rays of the dawn.

Though he held a weapon, his mind was free from crookedness; surpassing the sages through his pure conduct, he, being himself stainless, delighted the deer. For whom do virtues not strive to bring delight? BhKir 6.24.
He sent forth a breeze that blew favorably, with a gentle motion and wafting fragrance on all sides,
while setting aside the qualities of the season and bringing about a mass of light from the sun that led to comfort.
Causing the great trees to bend low by gathering their handfuls of fresh sprouts,
and providing the earth with soft grass every night so that it became a fit place for a bed.
By scattering drops of water from the sky as they fell and by calming the dust, he—
already deeply emaciated— was favored by his asceticism as if by a compassionate attendant through his service.

Beholding that auspicious omen before him, which was like a flower blooming for a great fruit, he did not fall under the sway of wonder; for the quality of majesty does not destroy the fortitude of those who have self-mastery.
Having obtained through their own merits that extraordinary wealth produced over many days— a splendor never known before—
the forest-dwellers, their minds overcome with despair, approached the abode of the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
Having been recognized and having entered with performed salutations, once the performance of their official duties had been relaxed,
they spoke at the appropriate time these delightful words to the Destroyer of the Mountain Clans.
O Maghavan, on this mountain, a certain sinless man, his body emaciated by pure bark garments, like one among the destroyers of darkness,
performs austerities upon the earth for your great victory.
He, whose arms are like terrifying serpents, bears a bow that strikes fear into his enemies on earth;
by his stainless conduct, which maintains virtuous behavior, he surpasses even the sages.
The winds are auspicious, the earth is covered with fresh grass, the sky is stainless, and there is a rain of water from the dust;
thus the host of elements, brought into harmony with his excellence of qualities, seems to offer him devotion.
The deer attend upon him without seeking to overcome one another, like courtiers attending a teacher;
and the trees bow down before him as he passes, for that mountain is subject to his will, just as a king is subject to his own.
His vast power proclaims his supreme form through his tireless exertion, as if manifesting victory;
yet at the mere sight of him, even though he is tranquil, people are seized by a fear born of his sovereign majesty.
Whether he be born of a lineage of sages or of a great family of kings,
we shall never be able to discern the whereabouts of you as you constantly practice austerities in the forests.
Or perhaps this was said by you out of modesty, having considered the many virtues [of our lineage] as a reason;
yet even this which is untrue, you ought to forgive us. Where are forest-dwellers like us, and where are your refined intellects?

Having learned from the host of Guhyakas that his beloved son was engaged in such pleasing austerities, Indra suppressed his rising joy; for the intellects of those who walk the path of policy are indeed powerful.

Then, having fixed his mind on devotion, Hari, though already known to him, acted as if he were unfamiliar; and in order to ascertain the steadiness of his discipline, he addressed these words to the celestial beauties.

What other weapon is there for victory over the Mind-born (Cupid), which— like you— is delicate, singular, minute, piercing the vital points, reaching great distances, endowed with infallibility, and without rival?
For the sake of ending existence, the water of awakening— which destroys the great darkness and pacifies the dust—
seems to reach exhaustion as it is drunk by you all with the cupped hands of your eyes.
In former times, the Creator of beings gathered together the loveliness found in various places throughout the world and fashioned you,
O fair-faced ones, thereby making the people worthy of the celestial chariots of the gods.
Therefore, go and obstruct his asceticism with your arts, accompanied by his ministers;
for surely, when those whose minds have been captivated by passion are opposed, it is easy to overcome one who is devoted to pleasure.
Without reflection, he desires through the slaughter of his enemies a delight in sense-objects;
for such is not the method for the cessation of existence. Where is the bow, and where is the path to liberation?
Be awakened to this, O Pṛthudāmā, and let there be no such transformation in you as that of other women;
for the minds of those who have descended as heroes, possessing their own glory, do not contemplate harm toward their wives.

Having received from her husband this command, which was preceded by the gods' desire for his honor and delivered in his presence, the assembly of celestial women attained supreme splendor; for the dignity of one who holds authority increases their brilliance.
Then, having performed their salutations, those women—whose limbs were bent by the weight of their breasts and who were filled with joy—set out for their homes;
the thousand eyes of the Lord of the Immortals became motionless, unable to behold that which surpassed the beauty of a lotus on a stalk.

Then, the sound of the drums, swelling as it issued from the openings of the vast celestial chariots of the ministers of the Lord of the Three Worlds— chariots accompanied by horses and elephants and guarded by divine maidens— announced the departure.
Emerging from the city of Maghavan, which was strewn with throngs of longing immortals, the suns—
blazing with radiance and positioned above the women— did not attain the quality of being surpassed by the royal parasols.

The flush upon the cheeks of the young women, produced by the rays of the hot-rayed sun, brought them the beauty born of passion; for their lotus-eyes were not yet fully opened due to the fatigue caused by the winds blowing directly against their ascetic garments.

As the multitudes of chariots stood still, somehow drawn by swift horses that had been pulled back through the power of the gods, their movement in the sky— since the rims could no longer turn— resembled that of celestial palaces.

Upon the breast-unguents of their beloveds, which had become pearl-like as the *tilaka* marks on their faces were washed away, there arose a sheen of perspiration that caused their hair to stand on end;
for even a transformation in beautiful things produces a charming ornament, and the outpouring of sweat from fatigue brings its own splendor.
On the path of the Maruts, the splendors of their banners and goads— shining with a uniform form, possessing the clear movement of flaming meteors,
and as pale-gold as the streaks of gold upon a touchstone— seemed to extend the distance by more than it was.

When the bodies of the women, which had surpassed the delicacy of flower garlands, acquired the power to endure the heat of the sun, the Gandharvas were filled with wonder; they returned [to their abodes], reflecting upon the auspicious and manifold variety of the Creator’s designs.
The celestial elephants, their splendor enhanced by vermilion and adorned with golden girths, exuding rut from their temples,
bore a resemblance to rain-clouds streaked by the glow of the rising sun, pouring down showers and flashing with lightning.
Having approached from afar that which is exceedingly difficult to reach— the very edge of the circle of the sun’s rays—
the armies proceeded toward the celestial river of lovely waves, which appeared like a single braid fashioned for the quarters of the sky.
Shaking the lotuses whose pollen was stirred up and which were crowded with swarms of intoxicated bees,
the breeze— cool as the waves of the celestial river— brought relief from the heat for the beloved women.
Having reached the earth and the rows of celestial chariots along the path by means of a tumultuous immersion of elephants and horses,
he first countered the swirling eddies of the divine river as its waters crashed against the edges of its banks.
As the chariots of those who had traversed the celestial paths according to the movements of the planets— chariots whose axles had scarred the altars of the divine mansions—
their rotations were seized without obstruction by the clouds, whose waters were agitated by the pressure of the rims.
The clouds, pierced by the tusks of the gods' elephants and pouring forth rain, brought relief to those tormented by heat;
indeed, for great beings devoted to the welfare of others, their activity is auspicious even when it causes them pain.
As the fine silken garment upon the hips of the celestial women was repeatedly tossed by the wind,
its broad network of rays from the jeweled girdle spread out in a curve, appearing like a pair of undergarments covering their thighs.
With their forehead-marks moistened by falling snow and dispelling fatigue, the clouds brought great delight to their beloveds; for even a small fault does not destroy much merit.
As he traveled through the sky, where the mass of clouds was severed and resembled a sandy bank with its rippling waves,
the rays of the gems on the celestial bow joined together to form a continuous line, as if they were the very limbs of the wives of the gods.
When success was achieved, the army of the thousand-eyed Indra, with conversations concerning their duties, having leaped over the path as they were eager to fly,
reached Indrakīla, whose peaks were shrouded by clouds.
Crowded with the lotus-faces of playful women, with the foam of raised, open, and bright parasols,
that procession— deep with the sound of musical instruments— shone as it approached the king’s head like a river from the sky.
As the chariots rushed forward with speed toward the canopy of clouds forming a bridge,
the horses— whose snouts were bent by the tightened reins— barely reached the earth as they were forced down with great difficulty.
The excellent elephants, descending from the sky toward Mount Māhendra with clouds resting upon their flanks,
attained a resemblance to the great serpents dwelling in the ocean, whose wings remain motionless as they take shelter within.
On the level and uneven slopes of the great mountain, as they traversed with the lightness of a flight through the sky,
the hoof-prints of the horses were found in their entirety upon the sandy banks of the rivers down to the very base.
On the mountain plateaus where waterfalls tumbled down the fair paths,
the sound of the chariots was heard with longing by the peacocks, who craned their necks in the expectation of deep thundering, as they were moved by the resonant echoes blending together.

In the midst of the sky, they beheld the stream of water flowing from the ramparts as if it were a woman separated from her lover, though she was joined by the dense, closely falling rays of the blue jewels near their base.
Enraged at the wind from the ichor of the nearby elephants, which had disregarded their own minds as they bore the yoke,
the celestial elephants— with their hearts captivated by their own female mates under some pretext— only with great difficulty permitted their departure.
Stirring up dense dust raised by chariot wheels along the roads— dust as red as fresh water—
the army spread across the forest thickets like the daughter of Jahnu (the Ganges) when its waters are agitated at the end of the summer heat.

Then his companions dwelt upon the earth of Indra, which was capable of providing enjoyment, near the Ganges; it possessed sandy banks of glowing jewels, was strewn with fallen blossoms, and was covered with lush, dense grass.
At that time, the encampment of the army of Hari’s friend increased the splendor of the earth even more than that of the king;
for what is difficult to obtain for those destined for great fortune when they are joined with prosperity, even by mere chance? It leads them to exaltation.

The splendors of the fragrant flowering trees, the secluded beauty of the creepers abounding in tender shoots, and all that was enjoyed by the celestial nymphs attained fulfillment; for such is true prosperity—that it benefits others.

Though exhausted, the women of the gods avoided contact with the sandalwood trees before them— trees whose sprouts were trembling from the breaths of hidden serpents and which, as if possessed by ill-breeding, seemed to be shrouded in concealment.
With their banners, blankets, and armor cast aside, the elephants— brought by those skilled in policy to relieve their fatigue—
shone like mountains overturned by the winds at the end of an eon, having dragged down the thickets of trees.
When the lordly elephant, having shed the sleep born of the fatigue of his journey, released himself from the mire of rut,
the chain at the edge of his bed appeared for a moment like a dark mass of mud that had dissolved there, fallen away due to his agitation.
Exerting himself, his path blocked by the torrent of the celestial river, the elephant— seeking to reach the bank fragrant with the ichor of wild elephants—
shook his head upon which a sharp goad was placed, and he paid no heed to his driver.
As the rider leaned forward, he raised his trunk toward the water remaining in the drinking trough;
as he wiped the reddish ichor flowing from his temples, a spray like rutting juice trickled down them.
Having smelled it for a moment, though he was extremely thirsty, the elephant— his eyes rolling in rage and fixed upon the bank—
did not even drink the cold water, as it was mingled with the spray from the rut-fluid of wild elephants.

Having wallowed in the waters of the river, which were fragrant with the ichor flowing from them, the lordly elephants emerged with their temples smelling of lotus and marked by streaks of copper-red hue veiled by filaments.
The water, thick with the dust of the army that was dark-red as a dense cloud, suddenly rippled upon its banks due to the commotion;
turned tawny by the pollen of lotuses crushed by elephants, it shone like a garment dyed with madder.
The majestic lordly elephants, their necks restrained by the forest guards and moving with graceful, rhythmic gestures as they lingered in the aguru groves,
attained a beauty like that of flowing, shifting boulders from their temples as they discharged streams of rut-fluid.
The wind bore along the fragrance of the elephants' rut-fluid, which flowed incessantly from their temples until it was entirely stilled;
its scent surpassed the aroma of abundant flowers nearby and was as sweet as crushed cardamom.

Resembling the deep roar of clouds, the trumpeting of the great celestial elephants spread through the marshy banks where the peacocks and chakoras were startled; these sounds were heard by the awakened and agitated lords of beasts.

The splendor of the trees growing in the city groves— possessing lovely furnishings that were stained with moisture, frequented by women weary from the fatigue of travel, and adorned with the various arrangements of dwellings— arose as if it were the beauty of forest trees.

Then, with a desire to leave the forest, the celestial nymphs abandoned their eternal city, which was as radiant as a palace created by their own magic, filled with blazing jewels, and possessed gate-towers like the bow of the Lord of the Gods.

As those lotus-eyed women, accompanied by sky-dwellers, entered the forest— each according to her station, illuminating the mountain slopes and creepers with their radiance— they assumed a uniform appearance, like flashes of lightning entering a grove.

The walking upon the earth following their journey through the sky brought great relief to the broad-hipped women; for the fatigue of their thighs and breasts had ceased, and the tinkling sound of their ornaments had begun again.

Leaving behind the trees that bore thick clusters of flowers easily plucked by the hand, the celestial beauties advanced toward those in front; for the desires of lovers regarding excellences always incline toward what is superior.
The forest-dwellers, whose bodies were as red as lac, whose sprout-like hands bore clusters of shimmering rays from their fingernails,
and who were captivated by the fragrance of unguents, attended upon the vine-like arms of the playful women.

With its clusters of blossoms being drunk by bees and its young shoots trembling, the Ashoka branch was seen by the women imitating the shaking of hands and the biting of lips performed by those in amorous passion.

O proud lady, do not labor in vain by shaking your hands that resemble fresh sprouts; why does this swarm of bees, having approached in the mistaken belief that they are celestial wish-fulfilling creepers, now flee from here?
"Abandon your anger; let your beloved be pursued, for your fickle mind will soon lie down with him.
Thus did the skillful circle of female friends conciliate a certain woman who desired to approach her lover.

The women who are the rivers, adorned with forest-groves as their breasts, are graced by riverbanks that are like charming wives— elevated with *kāśa* grass serving as silken garments and girdled by rows of warbling cranes.
The drops of water, having reached a state of division by falling from a great height, scattered from the current and spreading on all sides,
cool as the lap of a beloved and possessing the luster of pure pearls, were like the smiles of the forest.
The creepers, their forms bowed low as if gazing upon their circle of friends who showed them deep respect out of love,
possessed eyes of blossoms that spread wide with interiors streaked by the collyrium of steady bees.
The lofty plateaus captivated the hearts of the celestial king’s wives who had ascended them;
and the sandalwood trees, their dark luster enhanced by the rubbing of the elephants' temples reddened with rut, were likewise taken by the women.
Even though their own domain was present,
the women— enticed by the fruit-bearing shoots of the trees and wishing to do a kindness for the sky-dwellers— did what was pleasing to them out of affection.
