When her beloved offered her flowers with great insistence, the proud woman, addressed by him as "belonging to the family of another," said nothing at all; with eyes clouded by tears, she merely traced the ground with her foot.

O beloved, another woman, with her face upturned and her gaze fixed, her disheveled mass of hair loosened, offered no word; she did not even gather the garment she had cast aside in vain, nor did she realize that her sprout-like hand was among the flowers.

A certain lover was pressed against his broad hips by his beloved, who, with graceful ease, leaned forward and fastened a flower-earring upon him, her heavy breasts pressing against his chest as her girdle of clinging vines brushed against him.

With her waist-knot loosened by the weight of her hips, her chest graced by silken garments slipping from her breasts, and her abdomen—due to its extreme thinness—distressed with a line of hair clearly visible from the cessation of her menstrual flow; ||| BhKir_8.17 |||
With her mass of hair hanging down in disarray and her upper arms revealed, one woman,
under the pretext of gathering tree blossoms, respectfully captivated the mind of the lord of her heart.

A certain woman, her mind longing for her beloved, struck him on the chest with her breast— she who possessed high, full breasts— as he was apparently unable to clear away the pollen born of flowers from his eyes with the breath from his mouth.
When the flowers and tender shoots had been gently cast aside, with the words "these" and "those," according to her pleasure,
the beauty of the forest— as if abandoning the trees due to their lack of essence— placed its foot upon the women.
With sprout-like hands as red as coral shoots, with full breasts made pale by pollen,
and fragrant with the scent of flowers, the women assumed a bodily splendor that seemed like the very height of excellence of a tree.
With their beautiful thighs as stout as an elephant’s trunk, yet possessing the splendor of fresh sprouts,
their feet— though on level ground— were unable to move for a long time, as if stumbling at every step out of intoxication.
Their hips, possessing a captivating height and beauty through the radiance of the gems in their spreading girdles,
stood surpassing the splendor of fresh sandbanks with the excessive weight of their exhaustion.

Their bellies, endowed with beauty by navels situated near the waistline that were as tender as the calyxes of blossoming lotuses, assumed a downward curve at their middles— marked by the folds of skin— due to the excessive weight of their breasts.

Their faces were covered on all sides with lotuses whose rows of petals had not yet unfolded, which shared the same luster as their frosty ornaments, and which were speckled with drops of dew; likewise, their eyes remained unopened.
As the celestial nymphs descended along the mountain paths, their movements slowed by heavy perspiration, the forest-dwellers watched them with wonder;
meanwhile, the respectful gaze of the inhabitants of heaven first entered that place as if it were already filled with them.

Then the celestial river, resounding with the cries of swans, its lotuses shaken by darting fish and its mass of waves breaking against the mud-free banks, seemed to summon the bride to plunge into its waters.
The breeze, having subdued the heat and blowing gently, its touch caressed by the playful women,
moved within the rows of waves and, taking up spray, seemed to offer its hand as a support to them.

With their gait, the celestial women surpassed the grace of the *kalahaṃsa* swans; with the weight of their hips, the sandy banks of the river; and with their long-eyed faces, the lotuses—thus they cast aside all qualities of comparison.
The waters, which had previously been plunged into by the friends of Indra in rows of fish swimming toward their various boundaries,
were entered first by the celestial nymphs, who approached them with some trepidation.
As soon as the women had plunged into the water, their thick thighs supported them with effort;
the mass of waves, parting as it moved, scattered the cranes along the shores.
The waters assumed a turbid state, as if out of anger, their waves broken by the stone-like chests of the gods and the broad, swelling breasts of the brides, which acted like riverbanks.
With their hair disheveled, their garlands tossed about, and their sandalwood paste washed away,
the waves— having repeatedly committed offenses through excessive contact with the celestial nymphs— went into constant trembling as if filled with fear.

Those nail-marks, which were the uprooting of the minds of their rivals and were concealed by the ornaments of their amorous play, women bore as something else— like the remnants of saffron from a heart that had been stolen— and thus they became objects of boastful praise.
Are these two eyes of her with tremulous glances bees dissolved within a lotus petal?
Or are these her hair, with its mass of curved eyelashes, a swarm of bees motionless and silent?
"Is this a face with its filaments of teeth revealed by an unrestrained laugh, or is it a blooming lotus?"—
thus, after a long time, the women recognized their friend who had been hidden within the forest of lotuses.

No woman discarded the garland—though soiled by water—that her lover had woven and placed upon her full breasts in the presence of her rivals; for virtues reside in love, not in the physical object itself.
Without doubt, it was the collyrium applied by the women to ward off the redness at the corners of their eyes;
for even when that was washed away by the water, the passion [of love] dispelled the whiteness from their eyes, yet not their splendor.
Bearing their splendor like ornaments for women, they were as if carried away by the impetuous waters out of sheer greed;
submerged, they instantly became objects of pity, like ministers who have fallen from their office.
Beholding those beautiful women who, though lacking painted leaf-designs on their cheeks, red lac upon their lips, and collyrium in their eyes,
still possessed great splendor, the sky-dwellers realized that their own ornaments were merely decorations for their bodies, while the true adornment was the women themselves.
Likewise, the women of pleasure, out of affection for their lovers, had never before shown such regard for ornaments as they did when,
wet with water, they scorched the eyes of their rivals with the beauty of their nail-marks.

Those women with beautiful faces found no excellence at all in the waves— those who were like timid ones among the lotuses, whose dangling pearl necklaces resembled rows of shifting foam, and who were exceedingly fair-skinned amidst the saffron-stained waters.
Struck by the hands of women moving about in the lake water, it emitted a sound as deep as the resonance of a drum;
with its frequent thuds, it took up a charming dance, as it were, in keeping with the rhythm of the beat.
Adorned with reflections of faces smiling gently and laughing with splendor,
the Jāhnavī river attained the fulfillment of her favor by becoming well-disposed toward the wives of the king of the gods.
With their thighs brushed by darting fish, their gazes trembling with alarm,
and the sprouts of their hands shaking, the celestial nymphs became an object of sight even for their own female companions.
As if out of fear, the proud woman embraced her beloved when he was struck by a fish in the water; she gladdened him with joy.
For women captivate the heart even with feigned gestures, provided they are imbued with the essence of genuine affection.
With their hair-locks spreading out and becoming completely disheveled from plunging into the water,
the faces of the young women, their edges obscured, attained a resemblance to lotuses veiled by swarms of bees.
Shaking her hands, which were like fresh sprouts, as she was supposedly startled by the deep water,
the proud woman obtained an embrace of her lover’s body— a joy beyond reproach among her friends and untainted by her own lack of boldness.
Warded off playfully by the hands of their lovers, their breasts trembling with deep sighs,
and the sprout-like tips of their fingers shaken with graceful movement, the women in amorous sport attained the true meaning of the word "sportive."

When her steadfastness was cast aside by her lover who entreated her with devotion, the face of the lady with the arched brows— its eyes closed and its tears warded off by the water from his hands— seized the beauty of her co-wife’s face as it were.
When her hand was seized by her beloved who held water in it, the bride’s heart melting with passion,
her girdle— like a female friend— thickened by the water and loosened its fastenings, bore up her garment which had slipped from its gathered fold.

In the form of the one with arched brows, her side-long glances were stainless, her bud-like lips were free from red dye, and her tremor adorned her body; thus, even the offering of oblations became the very locus of her beauty.
As they submerged themselves near their beloveds with eyes half-closed and squinting,
their limbs trembling and their breasts heaving with gasps, it was unclear whether it was fatigue or passion that spread over them.
Sprinkled by her beloved for the last time, one woman grew angry with him as if he were an enemy; she was not appeased by his consolations.
For the heart of a person whose affection is deep-rooted, a certain indignation intensifies even toward a conciliatory gesture.

Having thus sported with women whose full breasts, thighs, and hips were so prominent that they pushed back the water, the river flowed forward as if uplifted by longing, its surface rising over the banks as it was crossed by the surging mass of waves.
Having led those pairs of cakravāka birds from one bank to another, thus robbing the lotus groves of their beauty,
the rivers shone like nights adorned with a canopy of stars, their pearl necklaces washed clean by the waters of the celestial river.

The ocean’s water bore the splendor of a bedchamber: its color varied by the infusion of sandalwood juice transferred from it, variegated by the rays of the clusters of gems from broken ornaments, rippling with waves, and having been used and then released by the celestial women.
Beholding the celestial women, their minds set on sport and adorned with variegated garments and ornaments,
the sun descended toward the western ocean as if to go there for the sake of pleasing them.
When the sun, resembling a central gem in a necklace and emitting shimmering rays, had departed from one side,
the sky bore the beauty of the day like a pearl necklace tossed about by its turning.
Having intensely tasted the honey of the lotus with his rays as if with hands,
the sun, becoming as if intoxicated and about to descend to the earth, bore a body that was crimson.
When the thousand-rayed sun had risen and was turning red before the eyes,
the heat departed from the earth and took refuge in the hearts of the cakravāka birds.
Lightened by its loosened roots and having abandoned its former position, the mass of rays, now gathered thickly in the western sky,
did not shine as the sun half-set, appearing as if weary and sluggish.
Like messengers from beloveds, the rays of the sun— copper-red with saffron— hurrying toward the evening circle,
were gazed upon with longing by women as they fell through the lattice-windows of the palaces.
Clinging with its exceedingly tawny soft rays to the trees upon the highest ridges,
has the sun entered the thicket of the western mountain, or the ocean, or the earth?
Agitated by the cries of flocks of birds in flight, its dawn-red glow not yet arisen,
the end of the day— pale as the sun’s horses— attained a likeness with the beginning of the day.
The western quarter of the sky, occupied by the twilight that shrouded the rows of clouds,
bore the splendor of the ocean colored by the glow of the coral-like waves of the setting sun.

Even as the people stood with palms joined and heads bowed, their hearts inclined toward him with love, the friendship of the unvirtuous— though once characterized by fickleness— ceased, as the twilight imitated it by fading away.
Fearing the heat of the dawn and finding the day’s radiance too intense,
the darkness gathered slowly from the lowlands and flooded the level plains.
No distinction could be perceived even in the greatest of beings, as if they had attained oneness;
the particularities of the worlds were absorbed into the Sun, as if fallen into its own self.
For those birds who desired non-separation from their mates throughout the night, their pairs were nonetheless overtaken by parting; indeed, the decree of Time cannot be transgressed.
Even when her mate drew near, the female bird withheld her speech from her beloved;
she was bowed down like a lotus flower, its joy abandoned, by the water-lily.
Have the various trees and mountains been dyed? Has the sky been bent down, or has it been covered?
Has the earth been filled in its uneven places, or have the quarters of the horizon been withdrawn by the darkness?
The lotuses, soiled by the arrival of night, abandon their bloom;
the splendor of the sky, with its stars clearly visible, has arrived. Everyone desires to dwell where there is no danger.
Released by the moon, the mass of rays— pale as the filaments of a ketaki flower and having attained its splendor—
spread across the quarter of Indra like a handful of scented powder.
As the king of stars drew near, the eastern quarter quickly cast off its darkness as if it were grief; adorned with the quality of clarity, she bore a face bright with the smile of her rays.
Resembling a blue lotus, the pale-white mass of rays falling from the moon— whose form was obstructed by the mountain—
shone in the sky like the waters of the Gaṅgā falling into the waters of the ocean.
The darkness, resembling an exceedingly dark cloud, obstructing the sky,
shone like the elephant-hide cast forward by Śambhu with his uplifted hand, being dispelled by his light of the opposite color.
When the mass of rays emitted by the moon, having moved near and far, abandoned its curvature,
the edge of the horizon shone as if breathing forth from the cessation of the burden of darkness.
With his radiance like that of pure coral, the moon dispelled the pervasive darkness,
just as the Primordial Boar [uplifted] the circle of the earth with his tusk, which was as reddish-brown as a golden chisel.
Then, illuminating the sky with its flood of rays, the moon— fair as a breast reddened by saffron—
slowly emerged from the eastern ocean like a golden pitcher.
The people gazed with insatiable longing upon the night, in which the moon had risen and the darkness was dispelled,
as they would look upon a newlywed bride whose face is partially revealed by her loosened veil and who is bowed low with shame.
The heavens were not brought to their accustomed clarity, nor was the darkness extracted from the forested mountains;
yet the face of every quarter was suffused with light, and the night was adorned by the cold-rayed moon.
Receiving the glances of proud women, turbid with warm tears,
the cool-rayed moon, having risen very slowly, departed toward the sky as if trembling with fear.
As the cool-rayed moon drew near his beloved star, the stars, emerging from the vicinity of her hand,
shone all around like a red-hued cosmetic ointment.
Impelled by the moon, that mass of rays dispelled even the densest darkness,
just as the Ocean of Milk, churned by Mount Mandara, dispersed the forests of thick and towering trees.
The shadows of the trees, rendered pale by the rays of the moon,
attained a resemblance to the floors of the dwelling-houses, which were variegated with white decorative patterns.

In the heat of the sun, together with his mate, the bird who was separated from her during the night could not endure the rays of the moon; for when the mind is afflicted by grief, everything becomes unbearable.
Carrying particles of raised dust and scattering the fragrance of blooming night-lilies,
the nocturnal breeze, with birds perched within it, rushed toward the rows of forest trees by the water.
The moon— with its mass of shimmering rays, marked by its spots, and bearing a blue lotus— was set aside by the maiden Night as a silver pitcher for the consecration of the God of Love.
Indeed, surely the Goddess of Victory does not approach one who lacks vigor or who is without a companion;
for even the Lord Anaṅga, though friend to the moonbeams, took up his victorious bow only when accompanied by her.
I envied even the celestial women, who, though their dwellings were graced by the beauty of artistic arrangements and who brought pleasant tidings through messengers,
yet remained close to their lovers and were already adorned with ornaments.
Neither garlands, nor sandalwood pastes, nor wines shone for women in separation;
for it is the union with the beloved alone that imparts loveliness to the instruments of pleasure.

As the proud women set out for the dwelling of their lords, disregarding the words of their dear friends and casting aside their fortitude, intoxication took hold of them as if it were bringing about their downfall.
As the women departed for the house of their beloveds, offering many messages for the sake of pleasure,
even their frequent stumbles— caused by their minds being utterly robbed by the God of Love— were generally of service.

The face of the woman who had hurried to meet her beloved quickly surpassed the unbroken moon in splendor; its cheeks were covered with thrills of joy, while its beauty took the form of decorative leaf-patterns and forehead marks.

"Let him be told everything that needs to be said; harshness toward the Lord is not fitting, my friend. Bring him back after conciliating him; for how can one who causes displeasure be brought back through conciliation? (BhKir 9.39)

"What is the use of going? It is not right to approach her. What pride, O beloved one who considers yourself so fortunate, can there be?"—in such conversations among women, lovers gathered together maintained a resolve rich with many nuances.

As a woman, her ornaments disarrayed, fell upon the chest of her lover— shedding drops of perspiration born of fresh union that caused her hair to stand on end— the very state of having her ornaments in disarray became her true adornment.
Among the amorous women who were distressed by drinking *śīdhu* liquor, he— having quickly subdued their pride and loosened their modesty—
was perceived as either Love itself or Intoxication when they were united with their lovers.
"The eyes are at the door, the hands are on the cheeks; where is her life?"—to lovers, these words, though repetitive, attained a fresh novelty for their delight.

Bending her pair of sidelong glances and obstructing the descent [of his gaze] upon her lover’s chest, the beautiful-browed woman created an ornament for herself; and at their union, her modesty came to an end.
The falling of tears, like a friend, checked the lord of her life as he set out at once with a step of anger, having been treated with deceptive disregard while distressed.

The dense bristling of his body-hairs signaled to the beloved that her proud resentment— cast aside through jealousy when she had turned away with falling tears upon being suspected by her lover— had now returned to its natural state as her heart was drawn toward him once more.
As her beloved passionately kisses the face of his beloved with its playful glances,
her garment slips from her hips along with her modesty, becoming loose as the girdle falls away.

Overcome with shame, the lord of her heart cast aside his lower garment, which had slipped from its knot and whose girdle was hanging loose; he embraced his beloved, who had bent forward so that the weight of her broad breasts formed a circle.
Embraces were honored by nail-marks, and kisses by the forceful striking of teeth;
thus, even in acts of love, desire alone possesses the fame for excellence in tenderness.
The shaking of sprout-like hands, internal hissing sounds, half-closed glances,
and faltering words in private became the weapons of Love for women.
The young men longed to drink the smiling faces of the women— which bestowed delight and possessed a flavor never before experienced— and the honeyed lotuses that stirred their thirst.
When the women of proud disposition had their resentment overcome by union with their lovers, and their quarrels pacified by tasting wine,
and peace was established between them, the Bodiless One (Kāma) did not fix an arrow upon his bow.
"Be quick to anger toward those whose hearts are bowed, and honor the youths who have provoked you"—
thus was the turn of wine savored by the young women like a manifold instruction.
Having tasted the exceedingly flavorful *vāruṇī* wine offered by their husbands with affectionate haste,
the young wives experienced— due to the absence of shame and confusion— was it a sharpness of wit or rather a clarity of heart?
Tasted by herself, then increased by her own longing, shared with her dearest lovers, and drunk together with them—
the wine of the young women assumed, at every step, as it were, a manifold variety of flavors.
The trembling of the ripples in the goblets, with their soft-glancing petals, assumed the grace of the lotuses as if to imitate the playful movements of the glances from the eyes of the young women.
For the lovers who delighted in the fresh sprouts of their lips as snacks,
the turn of wine became heart-pleasing through the cups of women’s faces, which were like full-blown blue lotuses of their eyes.
Even for one possessed of virtues, it is evident that the excellence of those virtues depends upon their receptacle;
for thus, the honey offered from the face of his beloved pervaded [his mouth] with an extraordinary intensity of flavor.

Beholding upon their jeweled goblets the excessive beauty of the decorative marks left by the teeth of their lovers, the young women considered the rounds of wine— which washed away the red dye from their lips— to be highly esteemed.
Having stolen the passion from the lips of Locanā and having perfumed her face with a distinct fragrance,
the wine seemed to effect a reversal and an exchange between the virtues of others and its own virtues.
Perceiving that the blue lotus, though identical in form to her eyes, was useless when placed upon her ear,
the flush of intoxication— like a friend who has gained favor with her eyes— distributed itself across them.

Although the juice of the lac-dye had been worn away by excessive drinking, the color of the bride’s sprout-like lower lip— its beauty enhanced by the marks of her lover’s teeth— attained an even greater intensity.

The beauty of intoxication, though present in every limb, was seen most intensely in the eyes born of passion and upon the surfaces of the cheeks as red as coral— as if it were concentrated in the faces of the women as they were in mirrors.
The wine of spring brought even those women who displayed the distortions of anger into a state of loveliness and favor;
everyone desires what is beneficial for their own side when under the influence of passion.

Causing the garments to hang loosely down to the navel, casting away shame, and provoking anger in men at the slightest pretext, wine wiped away the reproach of women by placing them on the side of virtue.

As the women cast themselves upon their husbands, their hearts—exhilarated by the intoxication of wine—were neither held back by shame nor did they abandon it; thus, that shame remained fruitless within them.

The intoxication of the young women, with its many virtues, eclipsed the natural grace of the bashful youth— grace that had been manifested through the dilation of eyes and speech during the embrace of the terrifying Raudrī.
A woman, though proud and full of the passion of love, went onto the lap of her beloved;
for wine, being unrestrained, indeed causes the disclosure of secrets regarding both virtues and faults.
Now that sweetness had been infused by honey and the movement [of passion] had been brought to full bloom,
the season for the flower-arrowed god to strike at amorous women shone forth as if newly aroused with passion.

Thinking, "May our lords, their minds deluded by intoxication, not depart from us to seek pleasure elsewhere," the women did not drink their fill of wine; for love perceives dangers even where none exist.
The cessation of mental agitation, solitude, the god of love, the intoxication of spring, the moonlight,
and union with beloveds— these led the passion of young women to an indescribable state.

In the amorous play of the proud women, where the proper bounds were transgressed by audacity and the flower-garlands in their tresses were ruthlessly disheveled, the flower-arrowed god of love fell into a state of utter confusion, as if intoxicated beyond measure.
When the bodies of the young women were overcome by the effects of drinking *śīdhu* liquor,
the amorous gestures of the lovers— though their aim was lost— shone forth, imbued as they were with the essence of passion.
Then, while the minds of those women were mutually impassioned and they were carrying out the command of the mind-born god— the friend of Hari—
the night, its latter half revealed by the sounds of awakening chants, seemed as if withdrawn and underwent its transition.

As the women were distressed by the prospect of an impending separation, the amorous dalliances of the young men— whose exhaustion from intense passion had been dispelled by sleep and who were awakened by the auspicious sounds of the morning trumpet— seemed to assume the very character of those former unions.
The night’s turning breeze, as if approaching very gently to massage the beloved women whose eyes were closed from the exhaustion of lovemaking,
revealed the scents of garlands and the enjoyment of wine within the mansions.

Upon the faces of the playful women— whose sprout-like trembling lips were scented with fragrance, whose eyes were slightly reddened and drowsy from sleep, and whose decorative leaf-patterns on their foreheads had been rubbed away— it was the residue of intoxication that established their beauty.
When the body-unguents had become visible only as nail-marks upon the copper-red bimba-like lips of the women, which had been sipped by their intoxicated lovers,
the splendor of the night’s enjoyment clung to the hearts of those women— distraught by separation— as a dear friend clings to her friends.
Then, having attained a splendor born of their own fragrance, those women— whose beauty was enhanced by ornaments set with gems and who possessed charming gestures—
abandoned their dwellings and went forth to entice the son of the Lord of the Gods.
As those broad-hipped women desired to move with quick steps,
their feet lingered long upon the ground due to the lightness of their gait and the weight of their heavy hips.
The earth, marked by the tracks of the brides with their soles stained by fresh red lac,
shone like a ground where blue grass and *ulapa* reeds have been reddened by *śakragopa* insects spread thickly over it.
The sound of anklets in the mountain caves, followed by the tinkling of broad girdle-strings,
was echoed throughout the forests, making them as resonant as the cries of eager swans and cranes.

The forests, filled with the enjoyment of gathering fruits yet devoid of deer because they were frequented by predatory beasts, spoke out on all sides to the sages; and the hearts of the women were overwhelmed by a rising sense of trepidation.
Through its possession by the king and the sage, that land captivated the hearts of the gods, ministers, and celestial nymphs;
for there is nothing that cannot be overcome by victorious ascetic powers invested with supreme majesty.
Then, as if with trepidation, those women, overwhelmed by wonder,
beheld upon the pure sands the superhuman footprints of Jiṣṇu, marked with his banner and adorned with the signs of his limbs.

The power of the sage was perceived by the young women through the abundance of trees and creepers— whose splendor surpassed that of the forest interior— even as they gathered his fruits and flowers, just as the season is perceived through the flourishing of trees and vines.

With its young shoots crushed by the celestial maidens and its branches bent by the weight of moist bark garments, the Aśoka tree attained great esteem; for even the state of being an attendant serves the purpose of those who possess true virtues.
With his limbs made firm by the practice of restraints and observances, he was seen by them holding his weapon—
exalted by the brilliance of incomparable tranquility, like the Atharva Veda with its established sequence of verses.
Surrounded by rays that spread across the sky and were as pleasing to the eyes as the moon, he—
dwelling on a single peak— seemed to bear the entire mass of mountain ridges upon himself.
On the celestial river, performing supreme penance with his great mass of matted hair bound in saffron,
he resembled the sacrificial fire upon the altar, spreading wide with its clusters of flames as it yearns for the oblation.
He possessed an effort commensurate with his immense form, an action beyond the reach of others that was consistent with that effort,
a penance as weighty as his actions, and a success equal to his asceticism that brought him victory.
Though emaciated by long-standing vows, he possessed the essential strength of a mountain; though devoted to tranquility, he was by nature difficult to approach.
Even dwelling in solitude, the sage shared the same splendor as the Lord of the Three Worlds, like a king accompanied by his ministers.
Beholding his body— which possessed the splendor of the essence of all worlds yet was emaciated, and which was capable of protecting the three realms—
the celestial women perceived that his exertion in the practice of asceticism was fruitless regarding its intended result of victory.
Having immediately enticed the sons of the sage and causing them to abandon their ascetic practices, whose strength was but slight,
they highly esteemed the significant office appointed for them by the wielder of the thunderbolt.

Then, as the young women desired to employ artificial charms to captivate the Son of Hari, the god of love suddenly descended upon their hearts; for the sweet splendor of youth indeed steals away the mind.
Instantly, at the command of the bride, by the friends of Hari, who played delightful lutes and drums,
the simultaneous presence of the entire cycle of seasons was manifested both in the sky and in the forest, each in its proper place.

The sky, filled with water-bearing clouds, shone brightly; the luster of the lightning-garlands attained full expansion, and deep, heavy roars, which interrupted the amorous quarrels [of the clouds], were spread throughout the quarters of space.
Immediately bestowing upon the buds of the *mālatī* flowers the splendor of the son of the Lord of the Suras,
the falling rain— though scattering drops— scattered the dust of the earth.
Touched by the wind, fragrant with the blossoming of *kakubha* trees, as it blew toward every direction,
the world of living beings— though its hearts were already born [to sorrow]— appeared as if newly come into being, yet its fortitude was gone and it was deeply agitated.
Though her heart was deeply pained, the young female cuckoo, delighted by the enjoyment of the ripe jambu fruit,
let out a cry made lovely by the fresh passion of her throat.

Though his mind was overwhelmed by the kadamba-scented breeze and the intoxicatingly sweet cries of the peacocks, Jishnu did not waver from his steadfastness, like an ordinary person; for indeed, it is not easy to break the concentration of the great.
Wearing a series of bracelets of lotus stalks, clad in the single silken garment of a grove of night-lotuses, and holding arrows in her hand,
Autumn— bearing a lotus in her palm upon her spotless surface— was embraced by the rainy season like a bride.
The cries of peacocks were surpassed by the calls of swans, the groves of night-lotuses by a rain of *kadamba* flowers;
having attained this extraordinary splendor, they served the great purpose of those possessed of great virtues. For union with the great leads to greatness.
Leaving behind the pollen-laden blossoms of the *ketakī* scattered with the dust from nearby *nīpa* trees,
the swarms of bees darkened the flower-stalks, which were bound in deep blue and possessed of sweet nectar.
Surpassing the closed buds of the bandhujīva flower on the grassy meadows holding droplets of water,
the large-bodied surendragopa insects attained the beauty of a mass of blooming palāśa leaves.

The winter season, though with its sparse frost-drops, attained for a long time a quality not born of its own time: it produced dense forests of flowering *phalinī* trees, and its breezes were fragrant with blossoming *kunda* flowers.

The son of Pāṇḍu felt no agitation at the blooming of the *lavalī* creepers nor at the joy-inducing breezes from the *lodhra* trees; for the mind of those desiring victory does not waver from its course of policy.
Adorned with the lovely blossoms of a few mango trees, its frost thinned and its *sinduvāra* flowers slightly awakened,
the season of Śiśira arrived— the sole kinsman of the God of Love— proclaiming the end of winter and the beginning of the fragrant spring.

Desiring to enter the groves of flowering trees, the Fortune of Spring, leaning upon a sprouting mango branch and with her anklets tinkling as she was adorned by swarms of bees, set foot in the lotus forests.

The celestial nymphs seemed to behold the bodiless Love-god, seated upon the shoots of the *aśoka* tree with his arrow in hand, smiling as he gazed upon the bride-like rows of *kurabaka* trees whose lips were blossoming flowers.
Constantly buffeted by the southern breeze as it blew upon her,
the swarm of bees on the lotus-plant’s face, spreading across the interior of its lotus-like countenance, took on the form of her own disheveled tresses.
The female *śāla* creeper, shaking her lower lip of trembling foliage as if out of fresh jealousy,
was kissed by a bee on the flower fragrant with honey, as if it were her face.
When self-protection through mastery over the senses prevails, an enemy is then unable to conquer;
for it was by thus conquering the world that the month of Puṣpa obtained victory over the one with the white horse, and not by means of flowers.
"How can you possibly have any regard for one who has been rejected by the sage along with the seasons?
Thus, with the blossoming of its jasmine flowers, the summer season seemed to smile at Spring.
Even a powerful force, when mutually opposed, is utterly unable to achieve victory over its adversary;
for at that time, the entire host of seasons, though capable of overwhelming the world, could not for a moment disturb his mind.
The lute-playing, pleasant to the ear, accompanied by his companions, and the seasons enchanting with their dense foliage,
aroused the god of love in the wives of the gods, who had not yet experienced the transformations wrought by the son of Hari.
Their eyes found no such delight in clusters of blue lotuses, nor in *yūthikā* flowers with their irregular leaves and clusters,
as they did in the limbs of the Son of Hari.

Those women who approached the Sage with the quality of their loveliness, desiring to bring him face to face, found that he himself aroused passion in them; for the course of purposes is indeed difficult to comprehend.

The eyes of the dancers, first cast playfully upon the white horse, did not move away from it— even though he followed the performance, nor did they turn toward his blossoming sprout-like hands with their unfolding fingers, which were not part of the dramatic representation.

A swarm of bees fell upon the foot of a celestial nymph—her mind intent on her dance—who was reddened by the application of lac-dye; they did so out of the suspicion that it was a freshly shaken red lotus.
The filaments of the kadamba flowers, with their tips bent down, bore away the thickly applied lac-dye from the feet of the languid dancers— like the very passion of their hearts incarnate.
The desire of the bride, whose slender form was concealed by the limbs of her attendants as she stood before the prince, became clearly manifest; for concealment itself speaks of one's longings.
When the garment on the hips of another woman was suddenly carried away by a strong wind, her thighs were exposed;
this startled even her rivals, who were filled with amazement at the modesty of the bashful lady.
Another maiden, holding a lotus stalk as a bracelet in her hand and resting her face— whose pale cheeks were stained with color—
upon it, gazed at the prince with eyes languid from intoxication, though she was not drunk by honey, due to the fever of love.
"O friend, bring my beloved here," she sent me forth, tormented by the arrows of the flower-bowed god;
for her heart, lacking discernment, did not previously perceive that you had already come into her presence.
Though she had long been unable to speak, her parched mouth failing her,
she nevertheless brought her virtuous friends' hearts to a state of moist sympathy along with their pairs of eyes.
Having abandoned her flower-bed, soft and fragrant, she longed for the earth covered with tender shoots;
and finding great restlessness there, she desired to come into your lap, which is so pleasant and cool.

Therefore, O sinless one, let her body have its desire fulfilled; for she will soon depart from this life for your sake. Indeed, penance is easily regained, but a suitable young woman who is full of affection is not found again.
"Abandon your hardness, or rather, grant speech; for the minds of sages are indeed tender with compassion.
Approaching him skillfully, a certain woman spoke thus to him who was disregarding one who had come to him.
Another woman, beautiful with her three folds of skin moving gracefully, her single hand busy binding up her hair,
cast the half-glance of her eye— the victorious arrow of the Mind-born god— at the son of the Lord of the Gods.
Clinging to a tall, flowering mango tree, a certain woman— her body bent by breasts as broad as an elephant’s frontal lobes—
raised herself up toward him like the staff of the Bodiless God’s bow with its string drawn back.
Another woman, having impulsively grasped her blue inner garment whose knot had slipped and which was fluttering about,
stood as if startled, though she was eager to run after him, held fast by the cord of her loosened girdle.

If there is peace within your mind, then why, O rogue, do you carry a bow? Sense-objects are dear to you, not liberation. Let it be; let the mistress of your heart grant no room in your heart to other women.
Having spoken thus with a sidelong glance and throbbing lower lip out of envy, she—
disregarding her elders, her honor, and her shame— struck him herself upon the chest with a lotus from her ear.
Approaching him with modesty, her cheek graced by the beauty of a single, slightly smiling laugh,
she gazed at him with an eye that was not fully opened, yet seemed to encompass him entirely as it rested upon her ear.
They spoke piteously, cast aside their shame, and shed tears before him;
for such is the extent of the means available to women to win back a lover who has become angry during a secret tryst.
Glances from their half-closed eyes, modesty, languor, extreme paleness, and despondency—these various states became their ornament; for the bodiless god of love has the power to adorn a bride.
Her gait was naturally as charming as the slow steps of an elephant and surpassed the movement of a female swan;
or rather, her eyes were half-closed with the fatigue arising from the great weight of her broad hips as she stood there.
The speech of the young women was confused, with words whose meanings were left unfinished due to the fainting caused by the falling arrows of the god of love;
and their glances, with eyes wide open and brows raised unevenly, were cast toward him.
Even that which was pleasing did not seem meaningful to the son of Pṛthā, who was pure in his steady concentration;
for when indignation burns the minds of the great, desire for pleasure finds no opportunity.
Having thus propitiated Indra himself with unbroken austerity,

the wives of the gods— whose splendor was destroyed as they gazed upon the daughter of Hari who desired the fortune attainable only by the total destruction of others— returned to their own abode with hearts full of agitation, their affection thwarted.
Then, out of indignation and by his very nature, as well as through that self-restraint of his senses,
Indra, the subduer of Paka, arrived at the hermitage of Jiṣṇu with a confident air.
In the form of a sage, he was seen before him by his son of similar appearance,
appearing as if exhausted from a long journey and having passed beyond his prime in years.
With his matted locks strewn about, white with a mass of hair gathered all around,
he was like the twilight at the end of the day mingled with the rays of the moon.
With his eyes having their outer corners curved and concealed by a pair of clear eyebrows,
he was like a lake whose lotuses have withered due to a spreading mist of frost.
Though his limbs were emaciated, they still bore the appearance of their former fullness;
though he was no longer young, he was supported by a staff as if by a virtuous wife.
O King, though concealed by his body, he shone with a splendor that overpowered the world,
like the sun whose form is veiled by a thin layer of clouds.
Though his body was aged, he possessed an extraordinary form;
having surpassed all splendor, he made his dwelling as if with trepidation.
The son of Pṛthā covered him from all sides with affection;
for even when a kinsman is unrecognized, the heart rejoices spontaneously.
Then, having received from his son the hospitality due to a guest, Hari rested upon a seat and spoke these words: "Bhārata."
It was well undertaken by you that you have begun this asceticism while still in your youth;
for even one like me, though advanced in years, is generally carried away by the objects of the senses.
Your physical form has attained a preeminent perfection of qualities;
for while beauty is easily found in the world, the acquisition of virtue is indeed rare.
The splendors of youth are as fleeting as the shadow of an autumn cloud;
the objects of the senses are pleasant at first sight, but result in torment in the end.
"The Ender (Death) is the one who besieges the living being whose misfortunes are continuous;
thus, while existence is to be abandoned, the mind of the fortunate one rises toward liberation."
"You possess a noble mind, since such a virtuous thought has arisen in you;
only your contradictory attire causes my mind to waver."
"Desiring to fight, have you perhaps put on this armor?
For ascetics wear only deerskins and bark garments."
Furthermore, what need have you for liberation while seeking to attain it, when you are indifferent to the body?
And what need have you for a great quiver and a formidable bow, since you do not seek to harm living beings?
This sword, terrifying to living beings like a second arm of Death itself,
does not permit peace for you while you are engaged in ascetic penance.

"Your Honor surely desires victory over your enemies; but where is there room for the mark of anger in one who possesses forgiveness? Where is there room for weapons in those whose wealth is their asceticism? (BhKir 11.18)
He who performs actions that result in death, though they lead to ultimate liberation and clear away the impurities of illness, is a fool who defiles pure water.
Do not nourish wealth and pleasure, for they are the root of faults such as violence;
indeed, these two are obstacles to the realization of reality that are difficult to eradicate.
By oppressing living beings to acquire fleeting riches,
one becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is the receptacle for rivers.

What among those women—who are accessible to those with virtuous companions, yet in whom there is weariness and from whom fear arises—is not a source of suffering, just as calamities are? BhKir_11.22.
By relying on fortitude, which gives rise to confidence, it is not difficult to overcome fierce enemies who are hard to assail,
nor to cast off enjoyments that are as harmful as snakes.
Fortunes never know their inner thoughts, nor do they ever become dear to those who possess them;
yet these fools remain attached to them, for living beings are indeed perverse by nature.
What blame can there be in words of praise when even among those lacking virtue, fickle fortunes cast aspersions upon the well-behaved as well? (BhKir 11.25)
In other bodies, the agent has likewise experienced both the union with the unpleasant and the separation from the beloved, which cause the mind to be distressed.
An empty place becomes crowded; misfortune is equal to a festival;
even separation leads to gain when there is a reunion with the beloved.
Then even pleasant things become unpleasant; then beloved ones become a thorn;
then even one's own life becomes a burden—when one who was once with kinsmen becomes solitary, deprived of what is dear.
If you, though disciplined, act with negligence and fall away from what is beneficial, you will suffer;
if you do not desire pain for yourself, then let no harm come to people through you.
Knowing that the stability of this living being is as flickering as fortune, do not destroy what is just; for the virtuous have justice as their foundation.
Abandon your zeal for battle; do not, through your asceticism, bring about destruction.
O you whose wealth is penance, become peaceful in order to effect the cessation of birth.
May the enemies within the body, such as the eyes and other senses, which are difficult to conquer, be subdued;
for when they are conquered, indeed, this entire world has been conquered by you.
Dependent on others for the accomplishment of his goals, base in conduct, and shameless, he who has not mastered his senses becomes subject to the control of men like an ox. (BhK 11.33)
"Tomorrow you shall remember this present experience of pleasure"—
thinking thus that desires are like dreams, do not fall under their sway.
Desires are trustworthy deceivers, dear yet doers of harm;
though they are difficult to abandon even when one tries to renounce them, they are indeed bitter enemies.
In this secluded mountain, which has been repeatedly flooded by the daughter of Jahnu, liberation draws near to you; do not raise your weapons against it prematurely.
When the Lord of the Maruts had uttered these words and remained silent,
he whose banner bears the monkey then spoke these words, profound with humility.
It is pleasing through its clarity, vigorous, weighty yet endowed with lightness;
it possesses expectancy, is free from embellishment, moves everywhere, and is unconfused.
Because its essence is determined by logic, it is, as it were, independent of scripture;
and because it cannot be shaken by others, it is comparable to the words of the sacred tradition.
Because it was unassailable by other people, it was as formidable as the agitated ocean;
yet, due to its nobility and the perfection of its purpose, it was as tranquil as the mind of a seer.
Who, unless they were of such a disposition, would utter these pleasing words— endowed with such qualities and providing an opportunity for practice— were it not for one whose intent is as follows?
O father, you have not understood the sequence of this effort of yours,
in that you wish to instruct me in the Dharma as if I were equal to the sages.
The speech of one whose continuity [of practice] is not understood becomes entirely fruitless, like the effort of one who opposes right policy, or like the words of Vācaspati himself.
"O father, I am not a fit vessel for these words of yours, however excellent they may be,
just as the night is not a fit vessel for a sky filled with clear stars."
I am the Kṣatriya son of Pāṇḍu, Pārtha Dhananjaya;
I stand under the command of my eldest brother, who was exiled by his kinsmen.
"By the command of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, I observe such a vow,
being intensely devoted to the propitiation of Indra, who is himself easily won over."
By the king playing with ill-fated dice, his kingdom, himself, we, and his bride have surely been staked as wagers; such indeed must be the power of destiny.
Without me, along with his younger brothers and Draupadī,
he suffers greatly during these nights that are so long and dark.
In the assembly, our enemies— who had already stripped us of our upper garments by force— further pierced our vital organs with words that cut to the quick, for we were overcome with shame.
In the presence of his preceptor, Yama instilled in his rivals a longing for the bringing back of Satyabhāmā,
as if it were a solemn pledge of truth.
For a moment the members of the assembly gazed upon her, who was led by Duḥśāsana,
like the shadow of a great tree returning at sunset.
"What is the use of looking at husbands who fail to initiate actions that fulfill one's purpose?"—
as if saying this, her eyes were filled with tears.
Our elder brother, who is fond of virtue, has endured our final state;
for while defeat at the hands of enemies is easy to obtain, censure from the virtuous is difficult to find.
The waters of the oceans and the minds of the wise are both clear; yet they are agitated when their stability is exceeded.
Affection for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra has given rise to enmity toward us; for friendship with the wicked leads to harm, like resorting to the shade of a tree on a riverbank.
The conduct of one who is fearless of censure, indifferent to virtue and vice,
and follows an evil path is as difficult to discern as the working of fate.
My heart would have instantly shattered had I been humiliated by my enemies,
if indignation did not provide me with the support of my arms for retaliation.
Having been cast aside by our enemies and reduced to the same condition as deer,
we feel shame even before one another, let alone toward those who dwell with us.
For a living being who is bowed down by a deficiency of power, who is devoid of essence, and who is exceedingly light due to the loss of pride,
his fate is the same as that of a blade of grass.
Beholding that which is unassailable and ever loftier among the mountain-like kings, do not fall into excessive fondness; for by what means can the greatness of the truly great be surpassed?
A man is attended by fortune for only so long, and his fame remains firm for only so long, as he does not fall away from his honor.
That man’s birth is truly meaningful, for when his name is placed first,
no other finger is reached by the hand as it is raised to count.
A mountain, though lofty and difficult to approach because of its dense forests, does not abandon one of great majesty who is tall with self-respect; for such a person remains unassailable.
They honor their ancestors; by them the earth is made true to its name, they whose brilliant glories put even the orb of the moon to shame.
An example [of this] is found among benedictions: "May you be the foremost among the high-minded, by whom indignation is cast upon enemies like a thunderbolt upon dry wood. (BhKir 11.65)
I do not seek pleasure nor wealth, which is as fickle as the waves of the ocean;
trembling at the devouring of impermanence, I seek the solitary state of Brahman.
I would wish to wipe away the mire of infamy created by deceit with the tears from the eyes of my enemies' wives, who are tormented by widowhood.
I may be ridiculed by the virtuous, or my intellect may be subject to error;
let your exertion be directed toward what is misplaced, or you may, if you wish, feel ashamed.
Without upholding the glory of the lineage by utterly destroying the enemies,
I consider even Nirvana itself to be an obstacle to the splendor of victory.
A man is as good as unborn, or even as a blade of grass that has perished,
so long as he does not recover with his arrows the fame that has been snatched away by his enemies.
O one rich in asceticism, tell me: how can there be the designation "man" for one whose indignation is appeased by the failure to conquer his enemies?
What is the use of the word "man," which relies merely upon birth,
when he who is praiseworthy for the virtues he has adopted is spoken of with wonder?
He whose name, when uttered by the assembly, is greeted with reverence as if it were swallowing up all vital energies—even his enemies rejoice; he alone is truly a man.
In accordance with his vow, desiring to retaliate against his enemies in battle,
the king meditates upon me alone, as if thirsting for a handful of water.
She was like a blemish upon a pure lineage, like a spot upon the moon—
she who, in times of distress, rendered her husband’s command futile.
How can one who speaks thus be considered a sage while obstructing the Dharma?
The sequence of the stages of life was remembered by the ancients; no deviation from it is recorded.
This burden has fallen upon me; my mother is far away;
it curtails my independence; and the king is my elder and a man of virtuous conduct.
They adhere to their own duty and do not transgress it even by enemies;
having been defeated, they flee, for these men of honor do not abandon the field of battle.
Either I shall dissolve upon the mountain peak like a scattered cloud vanishing away,
or, having propitiated the Thousand-eyed One, I shall extract the thorn of infamy.
Having thus spoken, Indra, manifesting his divine form, embraced his son with both arms and commanded him to worship Śiva—
the source of worldly existence— for the sake of prosperity and the destruction of sin.
"Once the wielder of the Pināka is pleased, you shall, together with me and the guardians of the worlds, possess a prowess that cannot be resisted even throughout the three worlds;
you will cause the prosperity of your enemies to greatly languish,"—having spoken these words, he vanished from sight.
Then, at the word of Vāsava, Dhanañjaya, whose face was radiant, performed austerities according to the prescribed rules in order to propitiate the three-eyed Lord who is free from weariness.
For that stainless one, garlanded with rays, who maintained victory and steadfastness and was never exhausted,
many lunar days passed on earth as he sat with only one foot touching the ground.

The son of Pāṇḍu maintained a steadfastness, like the lord of mountains, amidst the constant miseries that afflict the body and the senses; for the fortitude of the great possesses a power that is beyond comprehension.
His mind did not fall upon the fruits that were nearby and fragrant with ripeness;
for to those of well-performed deeds, the nectar-like water, pure and cool, acts as ambrosia.
He was neither amazed nor did he despond, nor did he repeatedly succumb to lassitude;
for his nature was one of vast fortitude, and the qualities of passion and ignorance were destroyed within him, as his power had been rendered feeble by the blow.
He bore a body emaciated by asceticism, which had overcome the rise of the three worlds;
for what indeed is not easy for the high-minded, even that which causes terror to those who know the truth?
At the end of the night, that victorious mountain appeared even more exalted than the blazing fire, surpassing the ocean in its quality of fortitude with its superior luster.
As he was constantly muttering his prayers in a whisper, the orb of the sun shone as if made terrifying by a halo, due to the rays from his teeth spreading out on all sides around his face.
Wearing his armor and with his strung bow placed upon his sacred thread,
he shone like the Lord of Mountains, his formidable peaks encircled by a great Indra-bow.
As he went to perform his ritual ablutions, Himavat bowed down at his footsteps like a cow before a weary traveler; for it is virtues that bring about greatness, not physical mass.
The radiant light, spread across the expanse of the sky and rising above his head as he stood with arms uplifted— difficult to approach— seized the paths of the sages and the gods.

Even during the nights of the dark fortnight, the splendor of the sky— joined with the contact of the moon’s rays— did not abandon its beauty, which dispelled the mass of darkness through the radiance of the prince.
In the stainless sky, the body of the sun did not shine, as if ashamed by the mass of great rays emitted from the one born of Jiṣṇu, which had eclipsed its own luster.
People beheld Rudra, whose matted locks emitted rays of rising dawn and who held a bow of exceeding excellence,
his forehead-eye as yet unmanifested, appearing as if he were desirous of churning the cities of the Asuras.
"Is he the lord of the Maruts, or the moon, or the fire with its broad crest? This man does not set out to perform a penance so difficult to accomplish. Thus did he perceive him through the ascetics.
The fire of the son of Hari did not burn the forests of trees, for it remained far away;
it did not reduce the waters to desiccation, nor was it easily endured by the perfected ascetics.

Then the great seers, being without refuge, sought the auspicious refuge of the Vinaya as virtuous men seek discernment, of the removal of delusion as logicians seek right reasoning, and of the ultimate limit as those without shelter seek a sanctuary.
Enveloped by rays that cast upward the circles of the sun's beams,
they were suddenly struck blind and were unable even to gaze upon Śambhu.
Then, having offered hymns of praise in order to bring face-to-face the Lord of the past, future,
and present, they beheld within that splendor a person of lovely form with three eyes.

He experienced the pleasure of touch upon the hump of the bull, which was adorned with his placed arms and possessed a full, non-slim circumference, as if upon the orb of Umā’s pair of breasts anointed with fresh sandalwood paste.
He stood upon the lofty peak of the snowy mountain, transcending the world,
as if pervading the entire universe with his splendor, including the paths of mountains, oceans, clouds, and the cardinal directions.
With his body draped by a great serpent clinging between his knees and thighs,
he appeared like the entire world encircled by the mountain that serves as the limit for the sun's rays.
With his broad, dark-blue throat— resplendent with shimmering rays, white as a mass of snow, and serving as a sacred thread—
he delighted the serpent [Śeṣa].
Bearing upon his head a white skull-cup filled with blooming jasmine flowers and with his hair bound up,
he bore the spreading radiance of the moon like the remainder of the waters of the celestial river.
Then the sages, having approached him face-to-face, signaled with a blink of their eyes and declared that the world was suffering intense distress produced by the asceticism of the son of Pāṇḍu.
Right there, O sole hero of the world, a certain man is performing austerities;
with a terrifying form, he overwhelms even the sun of stainless body, just as Vṛtra once did.

He carries a bow and great quivers, and wears a black, excellent armor; his matted hair, bark garment, and deerskin present this strange sight, which is consistent with the life of a sage yet does not fail to shine.

When he moves, the earth moves; when he restrains his organs, the sky, along with its directions and quarters, experiences a paralysis, as does the firmament together with its calm winds and its host of planets and stars.

By his power, he has conquered the very essence of this entire universe, including that which is possessed by the gods and the sons of Diti; for what is there that is not difficult for those who practice austerity to achieve?
Whether he desires to conquer the worlds simultaneously, or wishes to withdraw them,
or longs to attain non-existence— his splendors are not for us to endure.
Why do you remain indifferent? Speak, O Lord! There is nothing whatsoever unknown to you.
You, the Giver of Fearlessness, are capable of protecting us; while you rule, let there be no defeat for your devotees.
When the sages had thus addressed the cow and ceased speaking,
the Destroyer of Andhaka took up his speech, making the hollows of the quarters resound with a voice as deep as the roar of the waters of the divided ocean.
Do not think otherwise of him who is devoted to dwelling in the Badarī hermitage;
he is a man who has descended to earth as an incarnation of the Primordial Being, the source of the origin and dissolution of the worlds.
Desiring to utterly destroy his enemies who torment the entire world and whose strength is equal to that of the wielder of the thunderbolt, he has performed great penance as my worshiper.
And this Acyuta, by the word of the Lotus-born,
having descended to the earth to protect his subjects through the destruction of the Asuras, now dwells among men as a powerful being.
Realizing that this task is well-executed and skillful, the Dānava Mūka is rushing forward in haste to slay the son of Pāṇḍu; therefore, let us go there together with him.
Even though he cannot overcome him while he is unhidden, this one,
devoted to evil, confidently resolves upon victory through the illusory form of a boar.
When my enemy— whose body was a mere mockery of the King of Kirātas— has been slain by me with a released,
sharpened arrow, he will forcibly engage in this dispute regarding the hunt.
Behold the incomparable strength of his arms, produced by his own inner being, as he rages in battle— though emaciated by the pressure of asceticism and deprived of the abundance of allies.
Thus, having consoled them magnanimously with his chest— which was marked by streaks of uneven yellow sandalwood paste,
bristling with horripilation born of the heat, and adorned with strings of shimmering elephant-pearls— he spoke.
With a face like a flowering creeper, his long locks were bound by a fillet;
he bore the radiance of reddened eyes, and the surface of his cheeks was marked with streaks of saffron.
Carrying a great bow that roared like a thundercloud and was fitted with a single arrow,
the beautiful Śiva, commander of the Kirāta host, appeared like a mass of clouds.
And having reflected upon what was suitable for him, the lords of the Gaṇas assumed physical forms and marshalled a great army of forest-dwellers bearing spears, axes, arrows, and bows.
Then, having demarcated the forest regions on the mountain slopes by the command of the Lord,
they set out for the hunt, filling the vast earth on all sides with their terrifying roars.
With the cries of flocks of birds and herds of deer that were agitated, driven forth, and scattered,
the mountain, its vast forest caves filled to capacity, suddenly resounded as if out of fear.
The flock of beasts and birds on the road did not give way out of hostility;
for calamities, when they arrive together with many fears, instantly destroy even innate enmity.
Even when a powerful fear had arisen for the host of the Gaṇas,
the herd of camari deer regained their composure by clinging their broad and beloved young tails to the clusters of bamboo.

Even amidst the terror [of battle], the soldiers beheld their own troops rendered calm by lions whose manes were fragrant with the ichor of elephants and whose mouths were yawning at the moment of awakening.

The rivers bore waters reddened by the juice of sandalwood trees broken by elephants; their banks were made uneven by mud, and they were crowded with schools of śapharī fish that had turned away from their bellies.
The wind, fragrant with the ichor of buffaloes, aloe-wood, tamāla,
and nalada, and scattering flowers like crushed parrot-feathers, blew away the fatigue of the forest-dwellers.

Like the summer heat, that cataclysm of beings rendered the lakes— whose waters were churned up, whose plantains and wild millet were scattered and crushed, and whose lotus-stalks were withered— as if they had been ground by the force of a torrent.
Thus shaking the forest thickets growing on the peaks of Mount Acala,
the Lord of Umā reached the dwelling of the son of Indra, where the creepers were bitten by the teeth of joyful female deer.
Then he encountered that demon, dark as a rain cloud, who stood facing the sage and bore the body of a boar,
having split the earth with his tusks.
Having stationed his army on the banks of the celestial river, the illustrious Anshumat set out immediately after him, accompanied by a few excellent Kiratas,
remaining concealed among the thickets of trees and networks of shrubs.

Then the son of Mahendra, observing that the deer possessed a form equal to that of the loftiest mountains and was capable of great prowess in its flight, beheld it swiftly, its face fierce with steady tusks.
With his thick, bristling mane clearly erect, he rushed from afar, disregarding all other duties;
as the king’s mind was filled with apprehension, he repeatedly gave rise to this suspicion regarding the lion who desired victory.
With the roots of the śāla trees torn asunder by his thick trunk and the ramparts crushed by the friction of his dense body,
this solitary wanderer advances toward me, as if challenging me to battle.
In this place, by the power of my asceticism, beasts of prey have abandoned their predatory behavior toward others;
yet he displays it toward me even more intensely—could this be some transformation, or perhaps an illusion?
Or perhaps he has not been released by Wrath, who, like a grateful woman, was formerly served by him with great devotion;
having cast aside his hostile kin, does he now pursue me with speed, bypassing the other species of deer from afar?
"Surely this is no deer; it is someone seeking to kill who stumbles here, for my mind falters greatly.
A heart that is becoming turbid despite being pure tells of one's own well-wisher or an enemy."
"I am a sage, free from passion; whence can I have fear?"—this conceit does not lead to prosperity.
For what indeed is there that cannot be overcome by those of evil soul who harbor envy toward the success of others?
"Is this a Danava or a night-stalking Rakshasa? No, O Vanaja, there is no such strength in any creature;
for this one, dark as a cloud, having overwhelmed it, seems to make the entire king of mountains tremble."
This very same one, desiring the sacrifice of the hunt, while I stood peaceful and ready to strike him with my power of illusion,
caused the forests to become filled with startled and bewildered deer by means of the vast streams flowing from his army's banners.
Or perhaps, desiring to do what was pleasing to Suyodhana, who had been repeatedly honored by him,
he took refuge with that agitated and distracted host of forest-dwelling beasts, which had been stirred up by the assault upon the forest.
Has Aśvasena, his navel licked by the fire of the Khāṇḍava forest,
come here in his wrath to take revenge, or perhaps he has been provoked to anger by Vṛkodara?
Whether by means of my own strength or otherwise, I must certainly destroy anyone who harbors a mind intent on annihilation; for they say that the supreme gain is the crushing of one's enemies.
"O dear one, perform austerities for victory; do not give way to the wrong path," so the sage instructed me.
But it is not possible to protect the world otherwise than by slaying this powerful being.

Having reflected thus, he first grasped his bow, the primary emblem of manhood; and perceiving the enemy's vulnerability, he took up an arrow like a pure minister who has acquired the means to divide the foe.
By the powerful Dhananjaya, the bow was drawn with such steadiness that it became unerring;
though pressed even during the calamity of his own army, it attained a downward bend like a virtuous friend who bows in the face of distress.
Then, as the great arrow was being drawn back with a twang that split its hollows and was pressed against the ground by his foot,
the entire mountain fell into total uncertainty as it ascended toward the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Then, stationed within the circle of his firm, full-drawn bow, he was beheld with wonder by Śiva;
like the Creator himself, he appeared terrifying to his enemies as he prepared to bring about the destruction of the three cities.
And Śambhu, having drawn back his joined arrow, bent the lord of mountains by the force of his feet;
he released fire from the knot at the mouth of the bowstring, which was Vāsuki himself with his body stretched out as a bowstring.
As he was about to bring about the destruction of existence for the sake of existence itself, and the destruction of both white and black karma for the sake of their own purpose,
his enemy reached a state of ruin between them, like an *anubandha* (euphonic junction) situated between a root (*prakṛti*) and its suffix (*pratyaya*).
Then, having illuminated the path of the clouds and being irresistible because he terrified the elephants with his roar,
the arrow fell swiftly from the great Pināka bow like lightning from a massive thundercloud.

As he was proceeding, there arose from the great serpents a roar that split their hearts and ears—a sound so immense it raised the suspicion that the speed of Garuḍa’s descent had arrived. This great noise, born of their vast wings, rose up as a mighty echo.
For, proceeding even more swiftly than the mind from the eye of the wielder of the trident, his golden rays,
resembling shimmering streaks of lightning, created a path for the arrow in the sky.
Leaving the bow and departing toward the vicinity of Śiva through the openings left by those standing nearby,
the arrow was seen simultaneously entering the boar and, by its brilliance, entering the sky-dwellers who had gathered around it.
Against that enemy of the gods, who resembled a tamāla tree, he— his momentum unimpeded like a thick mist—
plunged toward the earth like a crocodile into a river, watched by those stationed in the sky who were overwhelmed with fear.
Instantly, with its beautiful joints and ridges, its cool iron claws for tips,
and possessing the splendor of the threatening finger of the enraged God of Death, it reached the sky, causing pain to the living beings among those who bore the monkey-banner.
Discharging his supreme weapon, which possessed a fierce brilliance like flashing meteors, he scattered it through the forests;
falling with great speed upon more than a hundred [enemies], he produced a roar like that of a mass of falling thunderbolts.
With his departure and flight unobserved, as if he had already reached tranquility through his extreme speed,
he pierced the mark before the movement of his mind could even arise, or rather, he did so without having even descended from it.

Like an effort striving to accomplish a goal set forth by destiny, that arrow— capable of swiftly achieving victory and seeking a target body pierced by the shafts of the bull-bannered god— was able to find its mark.
Like lack of discernment and futile exertion leading to ruin, like loss and greed destroying affection for one's kin,
or like misconduct and negligence bringing downfall upon a seeker of victory— the two arrows reduced him to exhaustion.
Then, about to enter the longest darkness, his strength suddenly failing,
he perceived with agitation that the sun was as if falling to the earth and that the ground was covered in a circle of trees.
Drenched in warm blood, his hooves and the tips of his fangs having torn through the rocks, he fell to the earth;
for a moment gazing at the son of Indra with his vital breaths still present, he let out a heavy roar of indignation and expired.
Then Pārtha, with abundant arrows, rushed at him with manifest prowess, desiring to seize that shaft;
for one who has already performed a heroic deed brings such pleasure to those who acknowledge his merit as one who is about to do so.
Like an act of assistance applied in vain when its object is absent, it vanished upon reaching the deer without achieving stability;
having exerted its power, it hung head-downward due to its own weight, as if filled with shame for its own prowess.
Having reflected upon him as he rescued her, and bearing his own supreme splendor like fame,
she seemed to loudly inquire after his welfare and embraced him fervently with both her eyes.
There, the long-armed one suddenly beheld a forest-dweller bearing a bow,
standing before him as if to present the command of the enemy of the flower-bowed god.
Having offered to the king’s son a salutation appropriate to his own birth, he began to speak these words in a conciliatory manner, motivated by a desire to persuade him.
Your appearance, which is peaceful, disciplined in mind, a vast abode of stainless austerity, learning, and wisdom,
proclaims a lineage as pure as that of the gods.
Illumined by the perfection of your majesty, you humble the kings with your dignity;
though a sage, you shine here as if exercising sovereignty like that of Indra.
The ascetic, too, having attained sovereign power, said: "You are the abode of all prosperity;
for your splendor is seen even without people, like that of one accompanied by ministers."
What wonder is there indeed in the glory of victory? Even liberation is not far from you.
For whom, having conquered the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, would the refuge of their desires not be attained?
Shaming with your brilliance one whose heat is not of the sun, you who are thus endowed with manly prowess ought not to take away this arrow of our lord, which was capable of piercing even a boar.
It is recorded that the eternal and righteous conduct practiced by the highest of men is for embodied beings;
if one such as you causes it to perish, tell me, who then would travel by that path?
Desiring to instruct even children in the great calamity that is the wrong path and how to turn away from it,
the ascetics— who have conquered birth and death through the power of yoga— cultivate excellent conduct.

Who would not find discipline dear to the virtuous, since it generates merit for those established in austerity, brings prosperity to those seeking happiness, and matures into liberation for yogins? (BhK 13.44)
Surely this arrow follows in every way the form of your venerable self;
by her, who has caused you—who no longer harbors any doubt that "this is he"—to set foot upon a wrong path.

O conscious one, you should not only be indifferent toward an arrow belonging to another when it has been taken up; you should also feel shame for killing a deer that was already slain by someone else.
The wise, ever listening with longing for those deeds by which they attain joy,
find even the mere mention of them— a source of shame for the proud man— even when they are recounted in jest.
How could he, paralyzed by his own lack of boldness, proclaim his own virtue as if it were the fault of another?
It is said that he indeed acts out of necessity; fie on this state of supplication, which breaks the dam of the wise!
It would have been difficult to speak against that, had not this deer acted with such force;
for the lord of the army would not have failed to strike him down swiftly with a sharpened feathered shaft.
Who indeed, other than the commander of the army, is capable of slaying with an arrow this tusked beast,
who possesses a body more solid than a mountain peak and is even more impetuous than a horse?
A friend is desired as one who assists in times of peril, and this lord of the earth is likewise such to you;
by opposing him, you have cast away gratitude, which is the sole abode of the virtuous.

For those desiring victory, the attainment of friends is the source of all prosperity; yet while a single good deed may be easily obtained, a protector is difficult to find for those whose wealth is hard to guard, and who seek a happy end despite their bitter conclusions.
Wealth is utterly fickle, and enemies may even seize the earth when it is in its highest state of prosperity;
therefore, do not despise this king, your friend, who has come to you as one as stable as a mountain.
"You practice austerities only to conquer; those seeking liberation do not take up weapons.
And you shall obtain the entire fruit of your asceticism by uniting with the king."
There is ground for swift steeds, a forest for the king of elephants, and abundant stores of jewels;
what need has he for this golden-winged arrow? It is simply that it cannot endure being bypassed.

One who is full of pride seeks to gain from others and undergoes a transformation even when there is only passion; but a great man, when entreated, does not strive even for his own life, much less for wealth as if he were a seeker of riches.
Let there be between you two, who have arrived by chance,
a profound mutual affection— fitting for those who rely upon one another— just like that which exists between Rāghava and the king of the monkeys due to the granting of each other’s boons.
It is not fitting for you to charge me with falsehood; what regard can there be for the arrows of ascetics?
For we possess other arrows against the king that rival the prowess of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
If you have need of arrows, why do you not request a husband from the mountain kings?
Having conquered the earth, would he not grant them to you, his friend and petitioner such as yourself?
Therefore, the sage—who possesses the wealth of beneficence—does not wish to grant what is asked in vain;
for he feels, as it were, the pain of a petitioner’s rejected request on behalf of those who are suffering.
Power over wealthy men either causes one to take what is desired by oneself or to feel love for them without fail;
yet for one who rejects these two causes, a request made to those of superior strength results in misfortune.

Having mastered the science of weapons in its true essence, whose else in this world endowed with the prowess of his own arms could it be said that his weapon has found its purpose among ascetics, were it not for the son of Jamadagni?
"O King, because of your munis' fickleness, you struck down this deer who was the possession of another;
yet he forgave that act, for ignorance indeed conceals the fault of those who are negligent."
Do not again commit this harmful act, which is contrary to your birth, appearance, and asceticism;
for misfortune, which defiles both worlds, befalls the evil-minded man who persists in the wrong path.
"You wish to sacrifice to the ancestors, yet you are currently intent on honoring the denizens of heaven;
O friend, since you are capable of granting even a path [to safety], why have you discharged your arrow at this deer?"
"You are a virtuous man; abandon this fickleness. For who indeed could always endure it?
Like the winds at the end of an eon, the unsteady disturb even the great, as if they were oceans."
Do not despise this lord of the earth as a mere mountain-dweller skilled only in weapons;
he was entreated by Indra himself to take up residence in these mountains in order to protect this world.
"This has been endured by me for the sake of the sage," said the commander of the army, as he offered his own arrow to the venerable one, saying, "May you too attain all prosperity."
Virtues attend upon oneself, prosperity arises, and calamities cease;
since such a meeting with the noble yields manifold fruits, how could one possibly fail to seek it?
Behold this king here within the trees, accompanied by armies with sharp weapons;
like a surging ocean with its waves restrained by a dam, he is held back by the laws of his covenant.
