O wise one, win over the mind of him who bears a strung bow more massive than that of the Lord of Serpents, and who, being most steadfast, surpasses the splendor of the banner of Indra; through friendship with him, you shall easily attain your desired goals.

Then, though struck by the Kirāta’s arrogant words as a mountain is battered by the waters of the ocean, the son of Pāṇḍu did not abandon his fortitude even when provoked; for the virtuous are indeed difficult to perturb in their inner hearts.
Having perceived the gestures of his enemies with subtlety, this skillful man, who had mastered the means of timing and was an epitome of the truth of extensive speech,
spoke words as if his agitation had been entirely stilled.
Adorned with the splendor of solitude, pleasant to hear, and gladdening even the hearts of enemies,
this eloquence— composed of clear and profound words— does not flow forth for those who have not performed meritorious deeds.
Among the wise, those are the most refined who place what is in their minds into speech;
and among them, only a few possess such perfected skill that they bring even the profound meaning to light.
Some wise men praise the excellence of the subject matter, while others praise the purity of the liberation [taught therein].
Since such inclinations vary for each individual, words that are pleasing to all are extremely rare.
O bearer of the burden, by you who have accomplished this speech through your virtues,
even though you are a forest-dweller, your self has been boldly placed upon the yoke of eloquent men.

Having employed the customary blandishments and displayed fears to divide his mind, and having assailed him with arrows in such a manner that the other [course] appeared as if it were the right course; BhKir_14.7 //

When he was about to act on what was contrary to your interests, why was the king not restrained by you? Indeed, a king who desires his own welfare must be directed toward what is beneficial by a dependent, even at the cost of his own ruin.
The destruction of a dispatched arrow upon hitting a mountain is certain; therefore, seeking it out is the proper course of action.
It is not right here to transgress against noble beings, for the violation of the virtuous brings about misfortune.
An incalculable number of stone-faced arrows were discharged at me by Agni when he desired to consume the Khāṇḍava forest;
yet, while I remained indifferent even toward the missiles of the immortals, how could I find any constancy against this arrow born of the mountains?

If the conduct of the noble is accepted as authoritative, why have we been rejected on the grounds of fault? For the speech of the virtuous, never before directed toward censure, speaks only of merit.

By disparaging virtues and attributing their opposites, the sword-like speech of the utterly arrogant and wicked man reveals his heart; for, concealing it while rending it as if in two, that speech betrays the inner being of the unrighteous person.
To whom do the deer dwelling in the forest belong? They are the property of whoever forcibly slays them.
Let the king’s honor in this matter be abandoned; for honor is not honored, whereas fortunes are ever-changing.
"The path must not be given to anyone at all—this is the vow ordained for me by the Great Seer.
This deer, seeking to kill us, has been slain by me; for the protection of one's vows is indeed the ornament of the virtuous."

How can a hunter, who has benefited himself by killing deer for his own sake, desire the asceticism of those who seek it? If you say it is out of compassion, let it be; but what recourse is there for the deer wounded by him, who thinks, "This was done by him before, not by me"?
When a sage, though unarmed, seeks to slay a living being, the compassion that arises toward him is the natural conduct of the great;
how then can he, who now bears a bow with arrow fixed, be regarded as one possessed of such compassion?
Moreover, that arrow was discharged by him for my sake, and its fruit is the destruction of his own body;
since I have taken possession of that unscathed [body], is not the commander of the army’s purpose indeed more fully accomplished?
As for what you said—that he should be asked for his desire—this is not appropriate for those of no small intelligence.
How could one who desires to seize by force find pleasure in royal splendors that have been defiled by the humiliation of another?
Having falsely accused you of hostile intent, the king forcibly seeks what is unattainable for you;
for even when one understands the cruelty of injustice, the mind becomes utterly deluded regarding its own downfall.
"Your sword, arrows, armor, and bow are not far away; what do you seek from the Lord?
Or if you have the power, then let it be done—by those who possess power, taking what they want by themselves is not a fault."
How can you call him a friend who, by mere whim, shows malice toward one engaged in ascetic practice?
For the wicked, whose intellects are opposed to the elevation gained through the acquisition of virtues, are by nature enemies to the virtuous.
Where are we, who are fit for the protection of the castes and stages of life, and where are these outcasts who slay the lives of deer?
It is not fitting for the great to associate with the base; elephants do not become friends to jackals.
When another person treats one with contempt due to the dullness of ignorance, that does not destroy the fortitude of the high-minded;
rather, it is an insult when one who is equal in vigor, lineage, and prowess exceeds [another].
When he quarrels, his fame is destroyed; when he practices loving-kindness, his virtues are disparaged.
Examining both possibilities, the discerning man treats the common person as one who is ruined by contempt.
For this reason, I have endured the hostile and insulting words of the hunter;
yet he shall come for the sake of an arrow and receive his deserts when he seeks to seize the crest-jewel from one whose gaze is poisonous.
Having thus signaled his intention and threatened with his splendor the horse of dark-blue hue for the sake of victory,
the messenger went into the presence of the Three-Eyed One, who was of serene appearance and had approached his army.
Then, at that reproach, the great army of the lord of the bannered host trembled with a roar,
like the mass of waves in the ocean when struck by the winds at the end of an eon, producing a tumultuous sound.

As if signaling haste for victory in battle, a fragrant breeze preceded the armies; its rows of banners fluttered and hung down, and it carried with it droplets of water from the thick clouds as it moved forward slowly.
Resonating with the tumultuous sounds of shouts of victory and war-cries, and the noise of bowstrings being struck against the palms to ward off elephants, that sound—
which could not have been contained within the bellies of the kings of mountains— spread through the quarters, making the earth tremble.
In the weapons of the forest-dwellers, whose forms were shattered by rays that had become intensely fierce in the night and which seemed to illuminate the space between the quarters of the sky,
the splinters flashed like the rays of the sun.
With his broad chest obscuring one quarter of the sky and his drawn, wide-circled bow,
the Lord shone as he stood in the midst of his virtues, like one who has spread out both wings to great length while remaining above them.

With equal prowess on both easy and difficult terrain, the hosts, desiring to go with speed in a race of "I first, I first," made the forest appear as if breathless and utterly agitated, being blocked by an unceasing flow.
The lands, which had suddenly assumed an excessiveness by concealing their hidden chasms, ravines,
thickets, and banks, were covered over by the Kirāta armies and for a moment seemed to regain their state of depression.

The mass of the leaders of the hosts, with its broad thighs and the expanse of their large creeper-like garments, caused the forests to seem as if they were being cast downward by the *śāla* and *candana* trees shaken by the force of their speed.
Then he appeared like a single elephant, proud yet emaciated by asceticism and as if withered by the flow of rut;
blazing for the destruction of kings, he was like the fire that consumes the quarters of the earth.

He was slowly casting his eyes— eyes that were tender because their retaliation had not yet been fulfilled— upon the ocean of the army with longing, as if toward a friend who, having carelessly taken up and held a single arrow, was favorable to his victory.
Seated upon his bow for the sake of remedying the calamity, he was like unswerving fortitude;
though remaining in his natural state, he was as unassailable and motionless as the ocean in a windless place.
He bore the appearance of Death itself as he approached the fanged beast that had fallen not far away after being slain;
before him, the twice-born had brought forward the sacrificial animal, like the Lord of Creatures himself summoned to the sacrifice.
By his own profound quality of fortitude, he had subdued the pride of others and brought it to great depth,
just as a forest in spring, with its thick and vast creepers, shrouds a lofty mountain in darkness.
With shoulders like those of a great bull, a full neck, and a chest as thick as a massive rock,
he resembled the Great Boar who, from the vast ocean, sought to uplift the earth burdened by a heavy weight.
Dark as a sapphire, with a majestic form, and outshining all embodied beings,
he stood as that ancient Person in human form, like the sun reflected in the water of a mirror.

Adorned with the fruits of the commencement of his master’s deeds, the hosts [of followers] approached him whose horse was not blue— the very course of the world-crushing majesty— just as clouds laden with water approach at the end of the summer heat.

Having previously boasted of their own prowess, the enemies, whose splendor had been blunted by the power of the sage, were in an instant rendered bewildered by helplessness; for one of great majesty destroys human effort.
Then they attacked there all at once, having relied upon the mutual strength of one another;
for even for those destined for great success, spiritual accomplishments are achieved only through the aid of companions.
Discharged from the broad bows of the Kirāta army, the arrows, having acquired great velocity,
flew forth together like birds with eager minds taking flight from a vast forest, their wing-sounds already set in motion.
The quarters of the sky resounded as if rent asunder by the roar of the bow, which, having swiftly reached the mountain ridges, was greatly amplified by its echoes within the deep caverns.
Shaking the thickets of trees and obscuring the edges of the sky and the quarters of space,
the multitude of arrows discharged by the host of troops produced a roar like a massive rain driven by the wind.

The arrows of him who had endured the insults of his first weapon fell as if they had already achieved their purpose— speeding down with impetuous force, released from his wrath, and terrifying the enemy host even as they were severed.

That defeat of Arjuna’s arrows— though they were adorned with the quality of straightness, had followed the path taught by their master, and struck at a time other than the joints of the bow— shook his resolve, just as the failure of virtuous men occurs even when they are well-prepared and follow the path shown by their teachers, yet at an inopportune moment.
The arrows of the Enemy of Smara, which cut through shafts, fell with their points turned downwards;
thus they immediately achieved an unbroken retaliation against the arrows of the Pāṇḍava.
The enemy struck far into the hearts of those attacking assailants, who were displaying great agility, with arrows that plunged deep into the agitated army of the seekers of worldly existence.
As his prowess surpassed [the enemy's] through excessive effort,
he, the destroyer of cities, discharged a profusion of arrow-showers by way of mutual distinction, like a summer cloud pouring down rain.
Not striking at any vital spot, these arrows— sent by one seeking his welfare and directed with auspicious intent— became a source of joy to the Sage, like the playful jests of a friend.
Seeing that his power with arrows was equal to or even superior to that of the enemy,
the Moon-crested Lord, whose own strength was rendered speechless by despondency, summoned his own crushing might.

The sun swallowed up all the masses of great arrows of Arjuna— who was exalted by the power of his asceticism and desiring to reach the further shore of the ocean of battle— just as the sun dries up waters.
Then Arjuna’s hand fell trustingly into the mouth of his empty quiver,
like a thirsty elephant’s trunk reaching for water left by another beast in a hollow of a mountain rock.

When that quiver had fallen— its essence of purpose destroyed because it was no longer needed for arrows— it suddenly encountered him whose affection had been rendered fruitless at that moment, as if desiring to attain a state beyond reproach by facing its former friend.
With his fingertips, he impetuously struck the two quivers back and forth;
his mind was eager for the path of action, just as the strategic application of policy and practice of one desiring to conquer the earth.
Arjuna, his form now appearing empty, bore those two great quivers which were devoid of their multitude of arrows,
like the crooked eastern and western oceans at the end of an eon, their waters completely dried up.
It was not because of that misfortune that Pārtha felt such regret for those two as he did because of their emptiness;
for the virtuous, casting aside their own calamity, grieve for those on the side of their benefactors who are submerged in disaster.
Because it was incapable of returning the favor, that hand departed from him with great difficulty,
like a nobleman leaving the family of a friend who has rendered assistance, even though that friend now turns his face away.
Then the subsequent action of her husband’s pair of quivers became as if a benefactor;
for when the expectation [of his return] was set aside, she had to remain in a state of boldness before her husband.
Śambhu, having cast aside his great web of arrows, pierced him in his vital organs with iron shafts,
just as one might refute an opponent with weighty arguments in the midst of a philosophical inquiry into the ultimate truth.
And before long, Caṇḍa stripped from him his armor, which was illuminated by the glow of flaming gems and marked with golden lines;
it was like a single dark-blue fragment of a cloud streaked with lightning torn away from a wind-swept sky.
Awakened by the thundering of the clouds and having emerged from the mountain cleft,
he assumed a brilliance like that of the night-fire when its smoke has vanished, yet devoid of its covering garment.

Even though they had attained a state of mindlessness, having reached that supreme height and fallen to the earth in his distress, those two quivers at that moment seemed to resume their connection with consciousness, as it were.
The Lord carved him— who stood like the sun in the pure sky, endowed with the splendor of asceticism and vigor—
with incessant blows of weapons, as Tvaṣṭṛ carves Vivasvat.
When his limbs, from which the impulse of agitation had been cast off and whose sensations were gone, became externalized,
the Sage’s own anger— like a repelling of iron— remained as if it were a heap of arrows that could not be counted.
Then the glorious one, whose arms were long, symmetrical, and rounded, his body smeared with dripping blood,
rushed forward with speed, letting out a roar and shaking the earth as it were with the blows of his heels.
Desiring to pierce Śambhu with his bow, which was white like a crescent moon and equal in power to Indra’s thunderbolt, he struck him as a great elephant strikes a clump of grass with its tusk.
As it fell, that bow-staff was brought to rest by the power of the one born from Bhava within himself,
just as the many-channelled river Sindhu, when raised up, was halted by Jahnu who stood firm in his majesty.

Deprived of his bow and thus pitiable in his actions— like a ritual service from which the noble spirit has departed— he was playfully cast far away by the wielder of the trident with feathered arrows that fell from no great distance.
Having attained the fruit of auspiciousness and guarding his heroic vow while dwelling in the hermitage of the forest of merit,
that sage, with his self restrained by those arrows of Śiva as if by prayers and fasts, performed his penance.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing his resolve, he took hold of that foremost stage— the very limit which is exceedingly difficult for others to cross,
the abode of the splendor of his majesty, like the supreme sword or manifest egoism itself.
Discharging arrows, he of faultless deeds moved with marvelous maneuvers through various paths;
bearing a sword in his hand, he was radiant like the ocean with its waves when accompanied by the sun’s rays.
Just as the thousand-rayed sun shines with its beams upon its own path and appears in the water as a reflection,
so too was he seen by all beings in the sky and swiftly upon the battlefields, clearly manifest in two forms.
Struck by an arrow discharged by Śiva, the sword fell from his hand— its grip-loose from the handle— with its blade blazing like the lightning-fire falling from a rain cloud.
With his bow drawn back, his net of arrows discharged, and his excellent sword severed, he was cast down in battle;
empty and exposed, he became like a region of the earth from which a garden has been utterly destroyed.

Having suffered defeat at the hands of his enemy, he was filled with indignation; and though he was alone with his two arms, desiring to conquer, he unleashed a rain of stones that shattered trees, like a torrent of liquid other than water.
When the canopy of rocks had been completely reduced to destruction by the arrows of the Lord of Beings,
the son of Indra hurled a mass of trees that filled the expanse of the sky and the quarters of space with their height.
With those trees, whose barks and heartwood were completely shattered and which colored the ground all around with their reddish sap,
the Lord [Śiva] seemed to offer a sacrifice to the deities of the stage, complete with flowers and sprouts.
Like a makara leaping from the river Amāra, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow rushed with speed toward the river of arrows and,
with both arms, struck the chest of the three-eyed god, which resembled a slab of gold.

The enemy of Smara (Śiva) endured the immodesty of the Pāṇḍava— who, desiring a means for valor and glory difficult for hostile armies to attain, had come into his very lap— just as Janaka, in his childhood, endured the misbehavior of his beloved only son.
Then, as the sage— armed with his formidable arms— advanced to the fray like a towering elephant,
Śaṅkara cast aside his bow and quiver and struck back with fists like thunderclouds.
The sound arising from the hands of Hara and Pṛthā’s son, produced by fingers joined with firm pressure, was as harsh as the crashing of many rocks; it echoed through the caves of the mountain.
The ape-bannered hero experienced, as if it were pleasure, the broad wounds torn by the blows of Śiva’s arms;
for who indeed could withstand even the imitation of those great-minded and courageous ones?
With his chest resembling the slope of a mountain covered by sprays of blood dripping from the openings of his wounds,
the Lord of Umā shone like a cloud bearing the fresh crimson glow of dawn.
The fists of Arjuna, repeatedly hurled against the chest of the wielder of the trident,
were repelled like the great waves of the Indus striking the broad shore of the Sahya mountain with violent force.
When the two long forearms of the Eyelike-a-Horse (Achyuta) fell evenly upon his neck,
the Diademed One (Arjuna), his gaze wavering as if from intoxication, stumbled after three or four steps.
Enflamed by a wrath that had risen from his sense of superiority, he rushed forward with great speed and power;
seizing the two arms of the one adorned with the crescent moon, he tore them apart with his own pair of arms.
Then there commenced a great battle between those two wrestlers,
who were proud of their heavy arms as weapons, a combat that caused the mountains to tremble and was formidable due to the complex interlocking of their maneuvers.

"Is this the Blessed One, or is it the Pāṇḍava? Is he standing below, mounted by the moon-crested Sage, or perhaps by Aja or Jiṣṇu?"—thus did the Gaṇas lose their senses through the force of their speed.
When the bull-bannered god moved, he moved; when he stood still, he stood still; when he bent, he bowed;
and when he rose up, he rose up—just as if the mountain, unable to endure the bull and the monkey-bannered gods, were repeatedly shrinking out of fear of non-existence.
As those two, having emerged from their chains of restraint, leaped gracefully while making sounds with their arms,
rivers— whose currents were blocked by the falling of their feet— flowed out and spread everywhere across the dry land.
As he was rushing through the sky with great speed, the ape-bannered hero, having intercepted him midway with equal velocity,
clasped the feet of that conqueror of the three cities, whose own feet were pressed upon the earth.
Startled at that deed, the Supreme Person, the destroyer of all karmas,
embraced the tireless one with his chest and crushed him to the ground as he desired to hurl him down.
The Blessed One did not experience such joy through asceticism as he did through the abundance of his noble character;
oh, for the virtuous, their own innate goodness, which surpasses the mere accumulation of qualities, is what truly brings benefit!
Then, beholding Hara, who was adorned with snow-white ashes, whose head was graced by a crescent moon,
and who bore a most enchanting form, the Pāṇḍava bowed down.
Seeing his own quiver, his bow, his massive body likewise clad in armor, and even his sword lying there exactly as it had been placed, he who moved with the gait of a bull was filled with wonder.
The clouds slowly showered the earth with water; wonderful celestial flowers descended from the sky;
the atmosphere shone intensely with stainless luster; and the sound of the unstruck drum pervaded the entire space.

The sky, filled with celestial chariots possessing radiant strings of jewels— belonging to those who had attained the state of the "Cleaver of the Lineage" (the Giver of the Lineage) and were protectors of the three worlds as he followed his course— shone as if it were covered with stars.
The great swans, the vehicles of the gods, with their throats adorned by tinkling ornaments as they flew,
seemed through their effort to embrace the sky with their outspread wings.
The bees, joyfully humming, spread out their swarms like garlands above him;
and as he sat upon the bull like a rain cloud, the wind refreshed the Lord.

"O you who possess steadfastness, praised aloud by the hosts of Gaṇapas with their hair standing on end, this is the most excellent fruit of penance that has borne its fruit: that you have thus offered praise to the Son of Hari. Thus was it said.

Having attained you, the supremely compassionate one who is accessible through devotion, people become victors over death, O Unconquered One; they become a refuge for the world, including its gods and asuras, in the face of fear.
Misfortune brings only despondency, yet one does not even desire the fulfillment of one's wishes;
nor do men bow down to a single man, O Lord, as long as obeisance is not first performed to You.
Men endowed with generosity and virtue practice [giving] while clearly perceiving the suffering of birth for the sake of liberation;
that you, being free from attachment, do not bow before those who seek a reward is purely out of compassion, not for your own sake.
That which is attained here without going far, and which bears fruit for one who has gone to the next world—
that sacred ford which fulfills all desires does not exist outside the ocean of existence except for you.
He who is full of devotion goes to the pure state, while he who is hostile goes to a terrible destiny;
O sinless one, O giver of boons, this is your supreme power over external signs, for there is never any change in your mind.

O Bhava, even for one possessed by passion, the remembrance of you— offered with devotion though they do not truly know your form as the one who bestows auspiciousness through the gift of liberation— leads to the cessation of worldly existence.
Having seen what is to be seen and performed what is to be done, the discerning person goes to a state liberated from misfortunes.
He who possesses right vision sees that which is supreme; he who worships you performs what is truly to be accomplished.
The sages, endowed with their own power, benefit living beings through instructions for their welfare;
yet you, whose majesty is inconceivable, utterly destroy the insurmountable karmas of one who has approached you.
O Compassionate One, you who transcend all illusion, you bear this wondrous form— an illusion that is impossible to remove, yet it removes the vast fear of miserable rebirths for all the worlds.
There is no lustful mind, yet there is supreme grace; there is no wife in your body, nor is there the god of love;
and yet you perform salutations at dawn to a donor—oh, how inscrutable this conduct of yours is by nature!
Your upper garment is an elephant hide with its entrails; your excellent girdle is a great serpent with blazing jewels;
your garland is a row of skulls; and your sandalwood paste is human ashes; yet these shine equally with a digit of the cold-rayed moon.
Though you are formless, by an incomparable cause you abide with a dual form that is both united and distinct;
such loveliness, even while wearing attire and ornaments of opposing natures, is seen in you alone among all beings in the worlds, and in no other.
Unlike the assembly of primary elements, you do not undergo birth, transformation, or cessation;
therefore, O transcender of all worlds, you have no counterpart in the world, nor are you comparable to anything else.
You are the ender of all things stationary and moving; by you, O God, the entire universe breathes.
You obstruct cause and effect for the yogis; you are the cause of the causes of causes.

Whatever unimpeded sovereignty has been attained in the worlds by Rākṣasas, gods, humans, or the sons of Diti—all that is the majesty of Pārvatī, who removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge; therefore, O Śiva, let this be an act of homage to you.
O Śiva, salutations to you in the form of the wind, who swiftly sustains the worlds, from whom the supreme and purifying Brahman resounds, and who completely purifies all misfortunes.

Salutations to You, the many-flamed Fire, who, for those who remember You and sit upon the ever-victorious seat consisting of Brahman, burns away the entire succession of the seeds of worldly existence.

Homage be to You, the source of seeds and the giver of life, who bestows Nirvana upon those long scorched by the flames of the fear of sickness and death through Your great fire of existence, by means of its arrival.
Salutations to You, the most excellent one who envelops all, yet remains unenveloped by any states of being; who is without beginning or end;
who transcends the path of the senses; and who, being of the nature of space, is unknowable.
Homage, homage to the most subtle one who sustains the universe; homage to him who stands near, and homage to him who is far away.
Homage, homage to you, the Lord of that [universe], who abides beyond the range of both speech and mind.
O Lord, you ought to forgive my ill-conduct, committed by me while lacking awareness;
for even those of evil soul who, having acted in opposition out of delusion, return to you, you alone are their refuge.

O Lord, O Master of Beings, grant me that sovereign power in battles by which I may attain victory over the host of enemies who have committed offenses against the son of Dharma— victory through that abundance of righteousness which is pure with faith and dear to those who follow the path.
When the son of Maghavan had thus spoken with his head bowed low, the Lord, having consoled him respectfully,
commanded him— the one who held the bow named Raudra and was surrounded by a blazing fire— to receive the Veda.

That glorious one with tawny eyes, bearing a formidable body through a splendor honored by the world, equipped with a triple-layered retinue and weapons, circumambulated the Lord three times while being praised with hymns by the hosts of gods; then he approached the heroic son of Pāṇḍu, as the sun approaches a rain-cloud.
Then, having obtained the permission of the moon-crested Lord, the world-protectors, led by the lord of the gods, bestowed upon him— who had his desires fulfilled—
victorious weapons of various kinds, while bestowing benedictions that yield unfailing fruit.

Having swiftly attained a victorious rise of such irresistible energy that he stood ready to bear the heavy burden for the sake of the world’s non-depression, the immortals, having established their station above him by his own majesty, sang aloud to him who was radiant with the glory of asceticism, as if to the sun.
"Go, conquer the world of your enemies," said Śiva, as he was praised by the hosts of gods while bowing at his lotus feet;
then, having returned to his own home, the son of Pāṇḍu, having secured the fortune of victory over his elder brother, respectfully saluted the son of Dharma.
